Azure Mastery turns those results into an on-device forecast, prioritises the next operational skill to revisit, and keeps the core study flow available offline. Optional sync uses your private iCloud account. The exam What is the AZ-104 exam? AZ-104 is the Microsoft Certified: Azure Administrator Associate exam — the credential most hiring managers expect when posting "Cloud Administrator (Azure)" or "Azure Sysadmin" roles. It's the natural next step after AZ-900 for anyone who administers Azure environments day-to-day, and the foundation underneath architecture ( AZ-305 ), cloud and AI security ( SC-500 ), and networking ( AZ-700 ) specialisms. Unlike Fundamentals exams, AZ-104 is hands-on and practical . It covers: Manage identities and RBAC at scale Implement storage with the right redundancy and access strategy Deploy and configure VMs, containers, and App Service Manage virtual networks and security groups Monitor a live environment, with Backup and Site Recovery in place for disaster recovery Expect questions that show you a Bicep file or Azure CLI command and ask you to predict the outcome. Microsoft updated the AZ-104 skills outline on 17 April 2026 , with minor updates to storage configuration, virtual machine management, container provisioning, and monitoring. Every question in Azure Mastery's AZ-104 bank is mapped to the current outline — no leftover questions on retired features. Read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Questions 40–60 questions, mixed formats Duration 100 minutes (120 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $165 (≈ £128 UK) Validity Renew annually (Associate) Format Online or test centre Skills measured · 17 April 2026 AZ-104 exam objectives Five domains, with weights set by Microsoft's 17 April 2026 update. Every domain below lists Microsoft's own skill groups verbatim from the official skills outline , so you always know which domain you're being tested on and where your weak spots cluster. Azure skill map Manage Azure identities and governance Published weight 20–25% 105 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Identity topics Manage Microsoft Entra users and groups Manage access to Azure resources Manage Azure subscriptions and governance Tests day-to-day Entra ID admin, RBAC scope assignment, and governance controls: Azure Policy, resource locks, tags, and budgets. Most candidates miss which scope a role was assigned at — subscription roles cascade down, resource-group roles don't reach up. Trace an assigned role from management group down to a single resource before exam day; scope is the recurring trap. Implement and manage storage Published weight 15–20% 104 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Storage topics Configure access to storage Configure and manage storage accounts Configure Azure Files and Azure Blob Storage Configuring an account correctly for a stated need — redundancy tier, access method, encryption — matters more than simply creating one. Candidates mix up four access mechanisms: firewall rules, SAS tokens, access keys, and identity-based Azure Files access. Pair each scenario with its access mechanism on paper first; the exam rewards distinguishing them, not naming them. Deploy and manage Azure compute resources Published weight 20–25% 133 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Compute topics Automate deployment of resources by using Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates or Bicep files Create and configure virtual machines Provision and manage containers in the Azure portal Create and configure Azure App Service Covers reading, modifying, and deploying Bicep or ARM templates, VM sizing and disks, containers, and App Service. Scale sets, availability sets, and availability zones get confused — each protects against a different kind of failure. Build one VM, one container instance, and one App Service app by hand; the exam tests configuration, not recall. Implement and manage virtual networking Published weight 15–20% 104 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Network topics Configure and manage virtual networks in Azure Configure secure access to virtual networks Configure name resolution and load balancing Work through subnet address ranges and public IP allocation before tracing a connection failure; each setting affects a different part of the path. Compare effective rules at the subnet and NIC, including priority and direction, before changing an NSG. An application security group only helps when an NSG rule uses it. For a Storage account restricted to selected networks, check both the subnet service endpoint and the account's virtual-network rule. Use DNS and route diagnostics to isolate other failures. Try a two-subnet lab: place a VM in each subnet, assign a public IP to only one VM, and inspect each NIC's effective security rules. Then restrict a test storage account to one subnet. If access fails, trace name resolution, NSG evaluation, the service endpoint and the account rule in that order. Record which control explains each result before changing a setting. Keep the matched rule priority and observed route beside your notes so you can explain the outcome from evidence. Monitor and maintain Azure resources Published weight 10–15% 75 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Monitor topics Monitor resources in Azure Implement backup and recovery Smallest domain by weight but often decides a borderline score: Monitor metrics, log queries, alerts, backup, and Site Recovery. Soft delete, versioning, and backup restore get treated as one control when they solve three separate recovery problems. Set up one alert rule and one backup policy yourself, then practise interpreting their output — that's what the exam expects. Common traps Where AZ-104 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared AZ-104 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Subscription scope vs resource-group scope Candidates read which role was assigned but miss the scope it was assigned at, so cascading access catches them off guard. Subscription-level roles cascade down into every resource group and resource inside it; resource-group roles never reach back up. Note the exact scope named in the scenario before you pick an answer — the role name alone rarely settles it. Soft delete, versioning, and lifecycle management aren't the same control These three storage features sound like one thing but each recovers from a different kind of loss. Soft delete recovers a deletion, versioning recovers an overwrite, and lifecycle rules only ever move or expire ageing data. Match the scenario's exact failure — deleted, overwritten, or simply old — to the one control that actually fixes it. NSGs and application security groups aren't two names for the same thing An application security group looks like a firewall rule on its own, but it filters nothing until an NSG references it. Of these two objects, the NSG filters traffic; the ASG groups VM network interfaces by role for an NSG rule to reference. Check for an NSG rule actually referencing the ASG before assuming any traffic is being filtered. Availability sets, availability zones, and scale sets protect against different failures These three sound interchangeable, but each guards against a different scale of hardware or datacentre failure. An availability set spreads VMs across fault and update domains; deploying across availability zones adds datacentre-level isolation, while a scale set manages a group of VMs and can autoscale it. Match "protect against a datacentre outage" to zones specifically — this is one of the exam's most common misses. Private endpoints add a private path; public access is a separate setting A service endpoint keeps traffic on the Azure backbone, but the resource still keeps its public IP unless firewalled off. A private endpoint assigns a network interface a private IP inside your VNet, but it does not automatically disable the resource's public network access. For a "no public access" requirement, use a private endpoint and disable or restrict the service's public network access; a service endpoint alone won't satisfy it. 6-week study plan Suggested AZ-104 study plan Build from identity and storage to compute, networking and recovery. Follow these six weeks of study blocks, then use timed practice to decide what needs more attention. Microsoft Entra ID Manage users, groups and licences. Review external-user access. Configure self-service password reset. Azure role-based access Compare built-in roles. Assign roles at management group and subscription scope. Practise resource group and resource-level assignments. Governance and cost Organise subscriptions and management groups. Apply Azure Policy, locks and tags. Set budgets and cost alerts. Storage accounts Configure accounts and compare access methods. Review redundancy and replication. Apply encryption and identity-based Azure Files access. Files and blobs Manage file shares, snapshots and soft delete. Compare Blob Storage access tiers. Configure lifecycle policies and versioning. Infrastructure as code Read ARM templates and Bicep. Practise modifying, deploying and converting templates. Use Bicep question drills to check your understanding. Virtual machines Practise provisioning, sizing and disk choices. Compare availability zones, sets and scale sets. Review encryption at host. Containers and web apps Compare ACR, ACI and Container Apps. Configure App Service plans and scaling. Review certificates, custom DNS and deployment slots. Virtual networking Configure VNets, subnets and peering. Compare NSGs, application security groups and Bastion. Review endpoints, Azure DNS and load balancers. Monitoring Explore metrics, logs and log queries. Configure alerts and action groups. Review Insights and Network Watcher. Backup and recovery Configure Recovery Services vaults and Azure Backup. Review backup policies. Practise Site Recovery failover testing. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Review explanations for missed questions. Return to domains that need more practice. Timed rehearsal Complete two 100-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review each run carefully. Identify recurring mistakes. Light review Revisit your key notes. Allow time to rest. Use your practice results to decide whether more study is needed.

The exam What is the AZ-305 exam? AZ-305 is the single exam required to earn the Microsoft Certified: Azure Solutions Architect Expert credential — Microsoft's senior architecture certification for the Azure platform. (The predecessor pair AZ-303 and AZ-304 were retired in March 2022 in favour of a single AZ-305 exam.) The Expert tier sits above the Associate-level AZ-104 and below specialty certs like Cybersecurity Architect (SC-100). Unlike AZ-104 , AZ-305 doesn't test your ability to configure Azure — it tests your ability to design solutions that satisfy a brief. You'll be given a multi-paragraph scenario (RTO/RPO targets, throughput requirements, compliance constraints, geographic spread) and asked which combination of Azure services best meets it. The exam aligns to the Azure Well-Architected Framework and the Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure — the same patterns Microsoft expects architects to apply on the job. Azure skill map Design identity, governance, and monitoring solutions Published weight 25–30% 113 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Identity topics Design solutions for logging and monitoring Design authentication and authorization solutions Design governance Tests recommending an identity, governance, or monitoring design, not configuring any one Azure resource yourself. Design data storage solutions Published weight 20–25% 91 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Storage topics Design data storage solutions for relational data Design data storage solutions for semi-structured and unstructured data Design data integration Clearing a stated RTO, RPO, or throughput number at the lowest cost is the judgement this domain checks. Read the numeric requirement first; it usually rules out half the storage options immediately. Design business continuity solutions Published weight 15–20% 83 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Continuity topics Design solutions for backup and disaster recovery Design for high availability Tests telling a backup and disaster-recovery design apart from a high-availability design for the same workload. Candidates treat backup and high availability as interchangeable even though they solve different problems. Ask whether the scenario wants recovery after an outage or continuous uptime during one. The exam is testing whether you can stop at the option that clears the bar, not the most feature-complete one. Read the numeric constraint first; it usually eliminates half the options before you weigh cost. Backup and high availability solve different problems A backup design answers how you recover after a loss, while a high-availability design answers how you avoid the outage itself. The exam is testing whether you'd choose zone-redundant compute over a Recovery Services vault for continuous uptime. Ask whether the scenario wants recovery after failure or continuity during it before naming a service. The Cloud Adoption Framework separates methodologies from workload-onboarding activities Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt, Govern, Secure, and Manage are the core methodologies. Migrate and Modernize are workload-onboarding approaches within Adopt, while assessment informs the plan. First identify the methodology, then match the workload activity the scenario actually describes. Do not treat assess, migrate, and modernise as peer phases in the framework. Authorising Azure resources and on-premises resources use different tools Azure RBAC authorises actions on Azure resources, while Conditional Access uses identity, device, location, and risk signals to grant or block access. Hybrid join and federation integrate identities; they are not substitute authorisation systems. Separate identity integration, access-policy evaluation, and resource authorisation before choosing a control. Check which resource and trust boundary the requirement names before answering. 8-week study plan Suggested AZ-305 study plan Practise architectural choices across identity, data, resilience and infrastructure. Use the final two weeks of this eight-week route for case studies and timed rehearsal. Identity and access design Review Entra identities, external access, Conditional Access and PIM. Design access to Azure and on-premises resources. Choose Key Vault approaches for secrets, certificates and keys. Governance design Design management group, subscription and resource group hierarchies. Plan tags and Azure Policy. Review Purview compliance and identity governance. Monitoring design Design Azure Monitor coverage across an estate. Choose Log Analytics workspace arrangements. Plan log routing. Relational data design Compare Azure SQL, Managed Instance, MySQL, PostgreSQL and Synapse SQL. Select service and compute tiers. Balance scalability and data protection. Data storage and integration Compare Cosmos DB, Blob, Files and Disks for cost and performance. Review Data Factory, Synapse pipelines, Event Hubs and Stream Analytics. Explore analysis with Synapse and Microsoft Fabric. Resilience and recovery Translate RTO and RPO requirements into recovery designs. Compare Azure Backup, Site Recovery and multi-region failover. Design high availability across compute and data tiers. Infrastructure design Choose compute and application patterns, including messaging, APIs and caching. Plan migration, configuration and automated deployment. Design connectivity, performance, load balancing and network security. Case-study practice Practise reading longer scenarios. Identify requirements and constraints. Explain why each alternative fits or fails. Timed rehearsal Complete two 100-minute simulator sessions with case studies. Review each run carefully. Track recurring design mistakes. Consolidate and rest Use Focus Weak Spots for remaining gaps. Keep final review light and allow time to rest. Decide whether your practice results support moving ahead.

The exam What is the AZ-400 exam? AZ-400 is the expert-level exam for the Microsoft Certified: DevOps Engineer Expert credential — Microsoft's senior DevOps certification spanning both Azure DevOps and GitHub. Azure Developer Associate retired on 31 July 2026; an Azure Developer Associate credential earned before that date still satisfies the AZ-400 prerequisite, but new candidates now reach it through AZ-104 (Azure Administrator Associate) instead. AZ-400 is the broadest exam in the Azure family by service surface — you'll be tested across five DevOps domains, with the build/release pipelines domain alone weighted at 50–55% of the exam. Expect dual coverage throughout: Azure Pipelines and GitHub Actions Azure DevOps Repos and GitHub repositories Bicep and ARM templates Security scanning — Microsoft Defender for DevOps, GitHub Advanced Security, Dependabot, CodeQL Monitoring — Azure Monitor, Application Insights, KQL queries Progressive deployment patterns — blue-green, canary, ring, feature flags via Azure App Configuration Microsoft updated the AZ-400 skills outline on 27 July 2026 with minor updates across all five domains — branching strategies, package management, deployments, IaC, auth/secrets, and monitoring. Every question in Azure Mastery's AZ-400 bank is mapped to the current outline. Read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Questions 40–60 multiple choice Duration 100 minutes (120 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $165 (≈ £128 UK) Validity Renew annually (Expert) Prerequisite AZ-104 (AZ-204 if earned before 31 Jul 2026) Skills measured · 27 July 2026 AZ-400 exam objectives Five DevOps domains, with weights set by Microsoft's 27 July 2026 update. The build/release pipelines domain alone is weighted at 50–55% — more than the other four combined. Each domain below carries Microsoft's own skill-group wording straight from the official skills outline , so you can tell exactly which domain a topic belongs to and where the gaps sit. Azure skill map Design and implement processes and communications Published weight 10–15% 68 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Processes topics Design and implement traceability and flow of work Design and implement appropriate metrics and queries for DevOps Configure collaboration and communication Tests tracing work across GitHub Projects, Azure Boards, and repositories, plus reading DevOps lifecycle metrics. Candidates memorise metric names without knowing which lifecycle stage, planning, delivery, or operations, each one measures. Match each metric to the specific lifecycle stage it reports on before picking an answer. Design and implement a source control strategy Published weight 10–15% 63 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Source Ctrl topics Design and implement branching strategies for the source code Configure and manage repositories A described team's workflow has to be matched against trunk-based, feature-branch, and release-branch strategies. Recovering or deliberately removing data from Git history often gets forgotten as its own examinable skill. Add history recovery and removal commands to your Git toolkit alongside everyday branching commands. Design and implement build and release pipelines Published weight 50–55% 271 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Pipelines topics Design and implement a package management strategy Design and implement a testing strategy for pipelines Design and implement pipelines Design and implement deployments Design and implement infrastructure as code (IaC) Maintain pipelines Fluency in both Azure Pipelines and GitHub Actions gets checked here, since a stem won't say which one applies. Knowing only one pipeline ecosystem leads to misreading a stem written for the other platform. Translate each pipeline concept into both YAML dialects, including whichever one you use less often. Develop a security and compliance plan Published weight 10–15% 60 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Security topics Design and implement authentication and authorization methods Design and implement a strategy for managing sensitive information in automation Automate security and compliance scanning Tests choosing between a managed identity and a service principal based on how long the identity must live. Swapping the two without noticing the scenario's lifetime constraint is the common mistake here. Ask whether the identity dies with one resource or must outlive it before answering. Implement an instrumentation strategy Published weight 5–10% 45 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Monitoring topics Configure monitoring for a DevOps environment Analyze metrics from instrumentation Application Insights telemetry and a basic KQL query against the logs are the practical skills under the microscope. This smallest domain gets under-revised, and GitHub's own alerts and insights get missed as a result. Review GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines alerting alongside Azure Monitor, not instead of it. Common traps Where AZ-400 candidates slip Four recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared AZ-400 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. The pipelines domain has two ecosystems, and a question won't tell you which one AZ-400 treats Azure Pipelines and GitHub Actions as equally examinable, not one as the real answer and the other a footnote. The exam is testing your working fluency across both ecosystems, whichever one is your day job's tool. Practise reading unfamiliar YAML in whichever pipeline platform you use less at work. Managed identities and service principals solve the same problem for different lifetimes A managed identity dies with the resource it's attached to, while a service principal can outlive any single resource. The exam is testing whether you caught the lifetime constraint behind the named authentication mechanism. Ask whether the identity needs to outlive one resource before choosing between the two options. Blue-green, canary, and ring deployments are not synonyms for gradual rollout Blue-green swaps all traffic at once, canary exposes a small percentage first, and ring moves through defined cohorts in sequence. A rollback or blast-radius constraint points to exactly one deployment pattern, and spotting it is the scored step. Define each pattern by its rollback behaviour, the specific trait that separates all three. A quality gate and a release gate check different things at different times A quality gate checks the build artefact inside the pipeline, while a release gate checks external conditions between stages. Placing an approval check as a release gate rather than a quality gate is exactly what's being checked. Match each gate to when it runs, inside a stage or between two stages, before answering. 10-week study plan Suggested AZ-400 study plan Follow this suggested ten-week route, adjusting the pace to your experience. Build from team workflows and Git to pipelines, deployment, security and monitoring. Finish with focused review and timed practice. Process and communication Plan work with Azure Boards, dashboards and GitHub Flow. Track cycle time, lead time and recovery time. Connect team documentation, wikis, webhooks and Teams. Source control Compare trunk-based, feature and release branches. Practise pull requests and branch protection rules. Manage large repositories, recover Git data and clean history. Packages and dependencies Publish packages with GitHub Packages and Azure Artifacts. Manage feeds, dependencies and artifact versions. Compare SemVer and CalVer; configure quality and release gates. Build pipelines Write YAML for Azure Pipelines and GitHub Actions. Choose agents and runners; configure triggers and stages. Reuse templates and add environment checks and approvals. Automated testing Compare unit, integration and load tests. Configure test tasks, agents and results integration. Use code coverage to identify gaps. Deployment strategies Compare blue-green, canary, ring and progressive releases. Use feature flags, A/B testing, slots and hotfix paths. Practise container and database deployments. Infrastructure and maintenance Deploy with Bicep, ARM templates and Azure Deployment Environments. Review Azure Automation State Configuration and Azure Machine Configuration. Monitor pipeline health, optimise cost and speed, set retention and migrate to YAML. Security and compliance Configure identities, tokens, service connections and permissions. Protect secrets with Key Vault, secure files and workload identity federation. Review Defender for DevOps, GitHub Advanced Security, Dependabot, CodeQL and container scans. Monitoring and instrumentation Connect Azure Monitor, Logs and Application Insights to DevOps tools. Review resource Insights, GitHub Insights and pipeline alerts. Practise metrics analysis, distributed tracing and basic KQL. Review and rehearse Revisit weaker topics with Focus Weak Spots and decay alerts. Complete two timed, 100-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review mistakes and use practice results to guide further study.

Questions 40–60 multiple choice Duration 100 minutes (120 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $165 (≈ £128 UK) Validity Renew annually (Associate) Format Online or test centre Skills measured · 27 July 2026 AZ-700 exam objectives Five domains, with weights set by Microsoft’s July 2026 update. Azure skill map Design and implement core networking infrastructure Published weight 25–30% 179 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Core topics Design and implement IP addressing for Azure resources Design and implement name resolution Design and implement VNet connectivity and routing Monitor networks Tests IP addressing, DNS, VNet connectivity, and routing as the foundation every other domain builds on. Candidates treat hub-and-spoke and Virtual WAN as always interchangeable regardless of how many spokes exist. Match the number of branch sites in the scenario to hub-and-spoke or Virtual WAN before answering. Design, implement, and manage connectivity services Published weight 20–25% 137 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Connectivity topics Design, implement, and manage a site-to-site VPN connection Design, implement, and manage a point-to-site VPN connection Design, implement, and manage Azure ExpressRoute Design and implement an Azure Virtual WAN architecture Site-to-site VPN, point-to-site VPN, ExpressRoute, and Virtual WAN are tested here as four separate hybrid-connectivity skills. A familiar VPN option gets picked even when the scenario's bandwidth or SLA requirement actually calls for ExpressRoute. Check the scenario's throughput and reliability numbers before choosing between VPN and ExpressRoute options. Design and implement application delivery services Published weight 15–20% 113 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Delivery topics Design and implement Azure Load Balancer and Azure Traffic Manager Design and implement Azure Application Gateway Design and implement Azure Front Door Tests choosing Load Balancer, Application Gateway, or Front Door for a stated global or regional requirement. Candidates reach for a regional service on a clearly global requirement, or the reverse. Look for the words global or regional and Layer 4 or Layer 7 before picking a delivery service. Design and implement private access to Azure services Published weight 10–15% 64 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Access topics Design and implement Azure Private Link service and Azure private endpoints Design and implement service endpoints Whenever public exposure has to be removed entirely, choosing a private endpoint over a service endpoint is the judgement call. Picking the cheaper service endpoint even when the scenario says no public exposure at all is the trap to avoid. Reach for Private Link whenever the stem rules out any public IP on the resource. Design and implement Azure network security services Published weight 15–20% 116 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Security topics Implement and manage network security groups Design and implement Azure Firewall and Azure Firewall Manager Design and implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) deployment NSGs, Azure Firewall, Firewall Manager, and WAF each do a different job, and telling them apart is the point. The WAF story differing slightly between Application Gateway and Azure Front Door is easy to forget. Check which product, Application Gateway or Front Door, the WAF question is actually describing. Common traps Where AZ-700 candidates slip Three recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared AZ-700 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. A service endpoint and a private endpoint restrict different things A service endpoint keeps traffic on the Azure backbone while the resource still uses its public endpoint. A private endpoint adds a private IP in your virtual network, but public access must be disabled or restricted separately when the scenario requires private-only access. The exam is testing whether you'd choose Private Link over a service endpoint when no public exposure is allowed. Reach for a private endpoint whenever the scenario explicitly rules out any public IP. Application Gateway and Front Door aren't interchangeable just because both do Layer 7 Application Gateway is regional, while Azure Front Door is global with edge points of presence and built-in caching. Cross-region routing calls for a global service over a regional one, and that swap is precisely what gets scored. Match global or regional in the stem to Front Door or Application Gateway before answering. Virtual WAN and hub-and-spoke solve the same problem at different scale Hub-and-spoke via VNet peering suits a handful of spokes, while Virtual WAN automates routing for large branch counts. The number of branch sites in a scenario decides the right topology, and that count is worth reading twice. Count the spokes or branches described before choosing between Virtual WAN and plain peering. 6-week study plan Suggested AZ-700 study plan Build networking foundations, then practise traffic delivery, private access and protection. Use the final study blocks of this six-week route for review and timed rehearsal. Virtual network design Plan subnets and IP addressing. Compare regional and global peering. Review gateway transit and hub-and-spoke designs. Routing and topology Configure route tables and user-defined routes. Review BGP routes and propagation. Compare hub-and-spoke with Virtual WAN. Azure DNS Compare public and private zones. Configure virtual network links. Review registration, resolution and conditional forwarding. Hybrid connectivity Compare site-to-site, point-to-site and VNet-to-VNet VPNs. Review ExpressRoute circuits, peerings, FastPath and Direct. Explore Virtual WAN hubs and branch connections. Azure Load Balancer Compare public and internal load balancing. Configure backend pools and health probes. Review NAT rules. Application delivery Configure Application Gateway routing, TLS and autoscaling. Review WAF integration. Explore Front Door caching, domains and global delivery. Traffic Manager Compare priority, weighted and performance routing. Review geographic, multi-value and subnet routing. Choose between Traffic Manager and Front Door. Private connectivity Distinguish Private Link, private endpoints and service endpoints. Review VNet integration for App Service and Functions. Explore Private Link Service across tenants. Firewall and network rules Review Azure Firewall rules, threat intelligence and Firewall Manager. Explore Premium IDPS and TLS inspection. Analyse NSG and ASG rules and flow logs. Web and DDoS protection Compare managed and custom WAF rules. Review geographic filtering and rate limits. Compare DDoS plans and mitigation reports. Target weaker topics Use Focus Weak Spots to identify gaps. Revisit core infrastructure and connectivity decisions. Review the explanations for missed questions. Timed rehearsal Complete two 100-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review mistakes after each run. Plan further practice where needed.

Azure skill map Describe cloud concepts Published weight 25–30% 109 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Concepts topics Describe cloud computing Describe the benefits of using cloud services Describe cloud service types Smallest domain but foundational: shared responsibility, pricing models, and picking the right service type for a scenario. Reciting IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS definitions is easy; matching a scenario to the model that actually fits it is the real test. Practise explaining a benefit like scalability or governance to a non-technical stakeholder — naming it alone won't be enough. Describe Azure architecture and services Published weight 35–40% 145 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Services topics Describe the core architectural components of Azure Describe Azure compute and networking services Describe Azure storage services Describe Azure identity, access, and security The largest domain: the architectural hierarchy, compute and networking basics, storage tiers, and identity concepts. Candidates skip the regions-to-management-groups hierarchy, but everything else in this domain assumes you already know where a resource lives. Learn identity and security concepts — Entra ID, RBAC, Zero Trust — at a describe level, not a configure level. Describe Azure management and governance Published weight 30–35% 130 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Governance topics Describe cost management in Azure Describe features and tools in Azure for governance and compliance Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources Describe monitoring tools in Azure Covers cost management, governance tools, deployment tools, and monitoring, all tested on purpose rather than mechanics. Learning how to configure a tool is beside the point here — the exam only tests what problem that tool solves. Match each governance or monitoring tool to the one problem it solves, not its configuration screen. Common traps Where AZ-900 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared AZ-900 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS: responsibility decides the answer Candidates memorise the three definitions without the responsibility trade-off that actually decides the answer. OS patching and other named layers each sit with either you or Microsoft, depending on the service type in the scenario. Match the scenario's described responsibility split to IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS rather than recalling a definition. Availability zones vs region pairs Candidates confuse surviving one datacentre failure with where data replicates during a regional outage. Zones protect against a single datacentre failure within one region; region pairs protect against losing the whole region. Match "one datacentre goes down" to zones and "regional outage replication" to region pairs. CapEx vs OpEx under the consumption model Candidates try to calculate a bill instead of recognising the CapEx-to-OpEx shift a scenario is testing. Retiring on-premises hardware for cloud consumption is the classic CapEx-to-OpEx scenario the exam keeps returning to. Read for a shift from buying hardware upfront to paying for use — that's the answer, not a cost figure. Azure Policy vs RBAC Candidates can't tell a configuration rule from an access-control rule in the same governance scenario. Policy enforces what a configuration is allowed to look like; RBAC controls who is allowed to act at all. Match "blocking a configuration" to Policy and "restricting who can create resources" to RBAC. Zero Trust is a principle, not a product Candidates look for a single "Zero Trust service" instead of recognising a security philosophy in the scenario. Zero Trust is a security philosophy Microsoft applies across its whole stack, not a single purchasable product or service. Look for verify-explicitly, least-privilege, or assume-breach language as the cue, not a service name. 2-week revision plan Suggested AZ-900 study plan Build a cloud and Azure foundation in the first week. Use the second week for focused revision and timed practice, adjusting the pace to your experience. Cloud concepts Study cloud concepts first. Use short practice sessions to check understanding. Review explanations before moving on. Azure architecture and services Review regions and availability zones. Compare compute and networking services. Explore storage and identity choices. Management and governance Review cost management. Explore Azure Policy. Compare monitoring tools. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Review missed questions and explanations. Revisit topics you have not practised recently. Timed rehearsal Complete two 45-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review each run carefully. Record topics that need more attention. Check your progress Complete another simulator session. Look for recurring mistakes. Use the results to plan any further study. Light review Revisit your key notes. Allow time to rest. Decide whether you are ready to move ahead.

Track readiness across all five domains, identify whether deployment, security, monitoring, optimisation, or recovery needs attention, and turn each result into a focused next session. Core study works offline on your device; optional sync uses your private iCloud account. The exam What is the DP-300 exam? DP-300 is the Microsoft Certified: Azure Database Administrator Associate exam — the credential hiring managers expect when posting "Database Administrator", "Azure SQL DBA", or "Cloud Database Engineer" roles on the Microsoft data platform. It's the natural next step after DP-900 for anyone whose day job has shifted from generalist data work into running and securing SQL workloads in production. DP-300 is the only Microsoft Associate cert dedicated to operating the SQL family on Azure. DP-300 is hands-on and operational . It validates that you can: Plan and implement Azure SQL Database , Azure SQL Managed Instance , and SQL Server on Azure VMs Secure data with Microsoft Entra authentication, Always Encrypted, dynamic data masking, row-level security, TDE, and Microsoft Defender for SQL Tune workloads via Query Store, automatic tuning, indexes, partitioning, and Resource Governor Automate operations with SQL Agent, elastic jobs, PowerShell, and ARM/Bicep Design HA/DR with Always On availability groups, geo-replication, auto-failover groups, and PITR Expect scenario questions that show you a query plan, a config snippet, or a recovery requirement and ask what you'd do. Microsoft updated the DP-300 skills outline on 24 April 2026 . Every question in Azure Mastery's DP-300 bank is mapped to the current outline — no leftover questions on retired services. Read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Prepare by building a deployment-target matrix rather than memorising one undifferentiated list of SQL features. Track what changes between Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, SQL Server on Azure VMs, and Azure Arc-enabled SQL Server: who owns patching, which job scheduler is available, where instance-level features live, and which identity crosses each control-plane boundary. Then connect operational evidence to the right tool — Query Store for performance history, Extended Events for event-level symptoms, elastic-job history for fleet automation, and backup or restore telemetry for recovery. That comparison habit is what turns DP-300's long scenarios into a small set of supportability, security, and recovery decisions. Questions 40–60 multiple choice Duration 100 minutes (120 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $165 (≈ £128 UK) Validity Renew annually (Associate) Format Online or test centre Practise the DBA loop Turn each DP-300 topic into an operational decision Start with one small workload and move it through the same sequence a database administrator owns in production. Choose its deployment target, document the service boundary, configure identity and encryption, collect a performance baseline, automate a repeatable task, and then prove how the database recovers. Keeping one workload throughout makes the trade-offs visible: an elastic job is not a renamed SQL Server Agent job, a database-scoped Extended Events session is not a server trace, and a failover-group listener solves a different operational problem from a manually failed-over geo-replica. Keep the evidence beside the decision. Save the query plan that justified an index, the Query Store interval that exposed a regression, the job execution row that explained a failed target, and the recovery-point and recovery-time numbers used to choose a continuity design. DP-300 scenarios often supply several technically valid features; the answer becomes clear only when you tie the requirement to the observable signal and the deployment target that supports it. Finish each lab by changing one constraint. Require the encryption key to remain outside the database engine, remove direct network access to the job database, delay restores on a log-shipping secondary, or place SQL Server under Azure Arc management. Re-evaluating the design after a single constraint changes trains the exam skill that matters most: explaining why a familiar SQL feature is right in one operating model and wrong in another. Skills measured · 24 April 2026 DP-300 exam objectives Five domains, with weights set by Microsoft's 24 April 2026 update. Every domain below lists Microsoft's own skill groups verbatim from the official skills outline , and Azure Mastery tags each question to its assessed domain so you can see which topics need more practice. Data skill map Plan and implement data platform resources Published weight 15–20% 77 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Platform topics Plan and deploy Azure SQL solutions Configure resources for scale and performance Plan and implement a migration strategy Tests choosing the right SQL deployment target and sizing its compute, storage, and scaling for the stated need. Candidates default to Azure SQL Database out of habit, even when the scenario names an instance-scoped feature only Managed Instance supports. Match the migration mode, online or offline, to the downtime the scenario says the business can tolerate. Implement a secure environment Published weight 20–25% 96 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Security topics Configure database authentication and authorization Implement security for data at rest and data in transit Implement compliance controls for sensitive data Matching an authentication, encryption, or compliance control to a named requirement across the three SQL deployment targets is the core ask. Transparent Data Encryption often gets reached for when the scenario actually needs Always Encrypted to hide data from a privileged DBA. Ask whether the requirement is protecting data at rest or hiding it from an authorised administrator before picking an encryption feature. Monitor, configure, and optimize database resources Published weight 20–25% 92 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Monitoring topics Monitor resource activity and performance Monitor and optimize query performance Configure database solutions for optimal performance Tests reading a query plan, wait type, or metric and picking the tool built to diagnose that specific symptom. Candidates reach for a dynamic management view when the scenario needs history that survives a restart or failover. Use Query Store for a regression that developed over time; use DMVs or Extended Events for what's happening right now. Configure and manage automation of tasks Published weight 15–20% 72 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Automation topics Create and manage SQL Server Agent jobs Automate deployment of database resources Create and manage database tasks in Azure Which automation tool is even available on the named deployment target is what trips people up first. SQL Server Agent is often assumed to run everywhere, but a single Azure SQL Database has no built-in Agent at all. Reach for an elastic job the moment a scenario names scheduled T-SQL running across a fleet of Azure SQL databases. Plan and configure a high availability and disaster recovery (HA/DR) environment Published weight 20–25% 88 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore HA/DR topics Plan an HA/DR strategy for database solutions Plan and perform backup and restore of a database Configure HA/DR for database solutions Matching an HA/DR feature to the stated recovery-time and recovery-point numbers matters more than recognising a familiar service name. Active geo-replication gets picked when the scenario actually wants a failover group's automatic failover behind one listener. Work out the RPO and RTO the scenario states first, then choose the HA/DR feature built to hit both numbers. Common traps Where DP-300 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared DP-300 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Azure SQL Database doesn't expose the instance-scoped feature set of SQL Server or Managed Instance. Linked servers, SQL Server Agent, and CLR are strong signals to consider Managed Instance or SQL Server on an Azure VM. Cross-database access is possible through Elastic Query external tables, not ordinary three- or four-part names. TDE and Always Encrypted stop different people from reading your data. TDE hides data from someone stealing the files; it does nothing to stop a DBA running a query. Pick Always Encrypted specifically when the requirement says even a privileged administrator must not see the values. Geo-replication and failover groups solve the same problem with different guarantees. Automatic, transparent failover belongs to a failover group; manual control is what geo-replication actually offers. Read the failover requirement for the word "automatic" before choosing between the two options. Dynamic management views reset on every restart or failover. Query Store, not a DMV, is what holds history that survives a restart. Save DMVs for a live, in-the-moment symptom and Query Store for anything asking about change over time. Azure SQL Database has no built-in SQL Server Agent. Elastic Jobs is Azure SQL's managed service for running scheduled T-SQL across databases; external schedulers are another option. Confirm the deployment target first: SQL Server Agent is available on Managed Instance and SQL Server on Azure VMs, while Elastic Jobs targets Azure SQL Database. 6-week study plan Suggested DP-300 study plan Work through SQL deployment, security, performance and recovery. Follow these six weeks of study blocks, then review your progress with timed practice. Choose a SQL platform Compare SQL Database, Managed Instance and SQL Server on VMs. Review tiers, elastic pools and Hyperscale. Plan compute, storage, scaling and deployment tooling. Plan migrations Compare Database Migration Service and Azure Migrate. Choose online or offline migration. Review schema and data migration tools. Authentication and roles Compare Entra and SQL authentication. Review contained users, server roles and database roles. Distinguish Azure resource RBAC from database permissions. Protect data and access Compare TDE, Always Encrypted, masking and row-level security. Review auditing and Defender for SQL. Configure firewall, virtual network and Private Link access. Monitor SQL performance Explore Query Store and automatic tuning. Review Intelligent Insights and Performance Monitor. Use dynamic management views to investigate performance. Indexes and statistics Compare clustered, non-clustered and columnstore indexes. Review filtered indexes and included columns. Manage statistics, fragmentation and index maintenance. Tune workload behaviour Review partitioning, In-Memory OLTP and Resource Governor. Analyse query plans. Investigate blocking and deadlocks. Automate administration Compare SQL Agent and elastic jobs. Review scripts, Logic Apps and Automation runbooks. Use ARM/Bicep and Azure Monitor alerts. SQL VM availability Compare synchronous and asynchronous availability groups. Review read-only routing and listeners. Explore failover cluster instances. Managed-service recovery Compare geo-replication, failover groups and zone redundancy. Review point-in-time restore, retention and geo-restore. Match recovery options to RPO and RTO needs. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Balance revision across the domains. Review explanations for missed scenarios. Timed rehearsal Complete two 100-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review each run carefully. Use the results to plan further study.

DP-700 — Implementing Data Engineering Solutions Using Microsoft Fabric — earns the Microsoft Certified: Fabric Data Engineer Associate credential. It's a role-based, hands-on exam for working data engineers who ingest and transform data and build analytics solutions on Microsoft Fabric. The audience profile assumes you're already fluent in at least one of SQL, PySpark, or KQL and comfortable with data loading patterns, data architectures, and orchestration. You'll work alongside analytics engineers, architects, analysts, and administrators to design and deploy data engineering solutions. This is not a vocabulary exam. DP-700 expects you to reason about real engineering decisions, covering: Full vs incremental load patterns Choosing between Dataflow Gen2, pipelines, and notebooks Transforming data with PySpark, T-SQL, and KQL Wiring up OneLake shortcuts and database mirroring Processing streams with Eventstream and Spark Structured Streaming Securing data with row-, column-, and object-level security and OneLake security Optimising Lakehouse, Warehouse, pipeline, and Spark performance Microsoft refreshed the DP-700 skills outline on 21 July 2026 . Every question in Azure Mastery's DP-700 bank is mapped to the current outline — no leftover questions on retired features. Read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Questions 40–60 (mixed formats) Duration ~100 minutes Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $165 (≈ £113 UK) Validity Renew yearly (Associate) Format Online or test centre Skills measured · 21 July 2026 DP-700 exam objectives Three domains, each weighted 30–35% as of 21 July 2026 on the official skills outline — there's no "easy" domain to coast on. Every domain below lists Microsoft's own skill groups verbatim, so you always know which domain you're being tested on and where your weak spots cluster. Data skill map Implement and manage an analytics solution Published weight 30–35% 108 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Implement & Manage topics Configure Microsoft Fabric workspace settings Implement lifecycle management in Fabric Configure security and governance Orchestrate processes Tests configuring the right Fabric workspace, security, and Git-lifecycle settings for a stated governance need. Candidates apply row- or column-level security when the scenario actually wants dynamic data masking instead. Match the orchestration tool, Dataflow Gen2, a pipeline, or a notebook, to the trigger type the scenario names. Ingest and transform data Published weight 30–35% 111 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Ingest & Transform topics Design and implement loading patterns Ingest and transform batch data Ingest and transform streaming data Picking a load pattern and a transform tool that fit the stated data volume and refresh window is the core skill here. A full load often gets reached for by habit when the scenario's volume and refresh window call for incremental. Match Dataflow Gen2, a notebook, T-SQL, or KQL to the skillset and store the scenario names, not the flashiest option. Monitor and optimize an analytics solution Published weight 30–35% 117 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Monitor & Optimize topics Monitor Fabric items Identify and resolve errors Optimize performance Tracing a failure to the specific Fabric item, pipeline, notebook, or shortcut named in the scenario is what's actually graded. This domain gets under-revised relative to its weight, since its breadth outpaces how often it feels tested. Learn the Lakehouse tuning levers by name: V-Order, OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, and partitioning each fix a different symptom. Common traps Where DP-700 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared DP-700 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Lakehouse, Warehouse, and Eventhouse are built for different workloads, not ranked by preference. Files-and-Spark, relational T-SQL, and streaming telemetry each point to one specific store, never a matter of preference. Read the scenario for its workload shape first, then pick the Fabric item built to hold that shape. A shortcut, mirroring, and a Copy activity move data in three different ways. A requirement for "no duplicated storage" points at a shortcut or mirroring, never at a Copy activity. Check whether the requirement forbids a physical copy before you reach for a pipeline Copy activity. Dataflow Gen2, a notebook, a pipeline, T-SQL, and KQL each own a different kind of job. The tool that matches the stated skillset and store wins here, whatever else looks more powerful. Name the store and the skill level in the scenario before choosing between low-code and code-first tools. A full load and an incremental load answer different volume and refresh constraints. Large volume or a tight refresh window in the scenario is what should point you at incremental loading. Look for a stated watermark or change-tracking need before assuming a full reload is good enough. RLS, CLS, OLS, and dynamic data masking each protect a different slice of the data. A requirement to hide values while leaving the row visible names masking specifically, not CLS or OLS. Match the protection to what must disappear: rows, columns, the whole object, or just the displayed value. 4–8 week revision plan Suggested DP-700 study plan Allow four to eight weeks, with extra time for SQL, PySpark or KQL if needed. Compare Dataflow Gen2, pipelines and notebooks; plan scheduled or event triggers. Ingest and transform Compare full and incremental loads, shortcuts and mirroring. Transform batch data with Dataflows, notebooks, PySpark, T-SQL or KQL. Explore Eventstream, Spark Structured Streaming and KQL windowing. Monitor and optimise Monitor items and configure alerts. Troubleshoot pipelines, Dataflows, notebooks and T-SQL. Optimise Lakehouse, Warehouse, Spark and query performance. Rehearse and consolidate Use Focus Weak Spots to revisit weaker topics. Complete a timed simulator session of about 100 minutes. Review mistakes and decide whether you need more practice.

It's a role-based, hands-on exam for working data engineers who integrate and model data, build and deploy optimised pipelines, and troubleshoot workloads on Azure Databricks . The audience profile assumes you can ingest and transform data with SQL and Python , apply software-development-lifecycle practices including Git , and are familiar with Microsoft Entra, Azure Data Factory, and Azure Monitor . You'll work alongside administrators, platform and solution architects, data scientists, and data analysts to design, deploy, and secure data-engineering solutions. This is not a vocabulary exam. DP-750 expects you to reason about real engineering decisions, covering: Choosing and configuring compute — job, serverless, warehouse, classic, and shared Creating catalogs, schemas, volumes, and tables in Unity Catalog Governing data with grants, row-, column-, and table-level security , ABAC tags, row filters, and column masks Modelling data with Delta tables, partitioning, SCD types, and liquid clustering Ingesting batch and streaming data with Lakeflow Connect, Auto Loader, COPY INTO, CDC, and Spark Structured Streaming Building Lakeflow Jobs and Declarative Pipelines with Databricks Asset Bundles Optimising Spark workloads with OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, and the Spark UI Microsoft's DP-750 skills outline is current as of 11 March 2026 . Every question in Azure Mastery's DP-750 bank is mapped to the current outline — no leftover questions on retired features. Read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Questions 40–60 (mixed formats) Duration ~100 minutes Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $165 (≈ £113 UK) Validity Renew yearly (Associate) Format Online or test centre Skills measured · 11 March 2026 DP-750 exam objectives Four domains, skills measured as of 11 March 2026 — the two data domains carry the most weight (30–35% each), with environment setup and Unity Catalog governance at 15–20% each. Every domain below lists Microsoft's own skill groups verbatim from the official skills outline , so you always know which domain you're being tested on and where your weak spots cluster. Data skill map Set up and configure an Azure Databricks environment Published weight 15–20% 79 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Environment topics Select and configure compute in a workspace Create and organize objects in Unity Catalog Tests matching a compute type, job, serverless, or classic, to a stated cost or startup-latency need. Every Unity Catalog object often gets treated the same, missing when a scenario needs a foreign catalog specifically. Learn which performance settings (autoscaling, pooling, Photon) actually solve the symptom the scenario describes. Secure and govern Unity Catalog objects Published weight 15–20% 80 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Governance topics Secure Unity Catalog objects Govern Unity Catalog objects Tests picking the right access control, a grant, a row filter, or ABAC, for the described governance scale. A single row filter often gets reached for when a scenario governing hundreds of tables actually needs ABAC. Check whether the scenario is protecting one table or standardising a rule across many before answering. Prepare and process data Published weight 30–35% 141 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Process Data topics Design and implement data modeling in Unity Catalog Ingest data into Unity Catalog Cleanse, transform, and load data into Unity Catalog Implement and manage data quality constraints in Unity Catalog Choosing a clustering and ingestion strategy that fits the stated table shape and update pattern is the core ask here. Candidates default to partitioning out of habit when a scenario's changing query pattern calls for liquid clustering. Match Lakeflow Connect, CTAS, or Structured Streaming to whether the source is batch or continuous. Deploy and maintain data pipelines and workloads Published weight 30–35% 142 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Pipelines topics Design and implement data pipelines Implement Lakeflow Jobs Implement development lifecycle processes in Azure Databricks Monitor, troubleshoot, and optimize workloads in Azure Databricks Choosing between a Lakeflow Job and a Declarative Pipeline for the stated orchestration or quality need is what's graded. Candidates reach for a bare Job when a bronze-to-gold flow needing automatic quality checks wants Declarative Pipelines. Learn to read the Spark UI for skew, spilling, and shuffle before assuming a job just needs more compute. Common traps Where DP-750 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared DP-750 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Managed and external tables leave the underlying data in different states when dropped. A requirement to keep the underlying files after a drop points specifically at an external table, not a managed one. Check whether Unity Catalog owns the storage before assuming a dropped table just removes a catalog entry. Liquid clustering, Z-ordering, and partitioning solve the same problem at different levels of effort. Liquid clustering adapts automatically; Z-ordering and partitioning both lock you into a fixed scheme upfront. Pick liquid clustering by default for a new table unless the scenario names a reason to partition instead. ABAC scales governance; a row filter or column mask is still the mechanism underneath it. A requirement to apply "hundreds of tables the same way" points at ABAC, not one hand-written rule. Reach for ABAC only when the scenario is about applying a rule at scale, not securing a single table. A Lakeflow Job orchestrates a workflow; a Declarative Pipeline builds and enforces the ETL itself. Automatic quality enforcement on a bronze-to-gold flow is the signal that points specifically at Declarative Pipelines. Reach for a bare Job only when the requirement is scheduling and chaining, not built-in data-quality expectations. Job compute and serverless compute trade isolation for a different cost and startup profile. Near-zero startup latency for frequent, short jobs is what should point you at serverless compute. Pick job compute when isolation matters more than startup delay for the described workload. 4–8 week revision plan Suggested DP-750 study plan Allow four to eight weeks, with extra time for SQL or Python if needed. Work through these flexible phases alongside hands-on practice in Azure Databricks. Refresh SQL and Python Review the language you will use most. Practise reading and modifying short examples. Revisit unfamiliar syntax before starting the main phases. Configure Databricks Compare compute types, runtimes, autoscaling and Photon. Configure libraries and access permissions. Create Unity Catalog catalogs, schemas, volumes, tables and views. Secure and govern Practise grants, row filters, column masks and ABAC tags. Review identities, Key Vault secrets and granular access controls. Explore lineage, audit logs and Delta Sharing. Ingest and model data Review Delta modelling, partitioning, SCD types and liquid clustering. Compare Lakeflow Connect, Auto Loader, COPY INTO, CTAS and CDC. Explore streaming with Spark and Event Hubs. Transform and validate Practise cleansing, transformations and merges. Apply pipeline expectations. Handle schema drift and data-quality failures. Deploy and operate Review Lakeflow Jobs, Declarative Pipelines, triggers and recovery. Use Git and Asset Bundles through CLI or REST workflows. Investigate Spark skew, spill and shuffle; review OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and monitoring. Rehearse and consolidate Use Focus Weak Spots to revisit weaker topics. Complete a timed simulator session of about 100 minutes. Review mistakes and decide whether you need more practice.

DP-800 is the exam that earns the Microsoft Certified: SQL AI Developer Associate credential (exam title: "Developing AI-Enabled Database Solutions") — the credential Microsoft introduced for the role hiring managers now post as "SQL AI Developer", "Database Developer (AI)", or "Fabric Data & AI Developer". It's the natural next step after DP-900 for SQL developers whose day job has expanded from classical schema work into shipping embeddings, vector search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) directly inside SQL Server, Azure SQL, and SQL databases in Microsoft Fabric. DP-800 is the only Microsoft Associate cert dedicated to AI-enabled data-tier development. DP-800 is code-first and developer-focused . It validates that you can: Design tables and indexes — including column store, in-memory, temporal, ledger, external, and graph — and choose the right constraints, sequences, and partitioning Write advanced T-SQL: CTEs, window functions, JSON shaping (JSON_OBJECT/OPENJSON/JSON_MODIFY), regex (REGEXP_LIKE/REPLACE/SUBSTR/INSTR), fuzzy matching (EDIT_DISTANCE, JARO_WINKLER_DISTANCE), graph MATCH queries, error handling Secure data with Always Encrypted, Dynamic Data Masking, Row-Level Security, and Managed Identity passwordless access Tune workloads via Query Store and DMVs Deploy with SQL Database Projects and Data API Builder Bring AI into SQL itself — generating embeddings, building vector indexes, designing RAG flows with sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint , structuring outputs with JSON Expect scenario questions that show a snippet of T-SQL or a chunking strategy and ask what's wrong, what's better, or what's required. Microsoft published the DP-800 skills outline on 12 March 2026 . Every question in Azure Mastery's DP-800 bank is mapped to the current outline — no questions on retired services or pre-AI SQL-only patterns. Read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Questions 40–60 mixed format Duration 100 minutes (120 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $165 (≈ £128 UK) Validity Renew annually (Associate) Format Online or test centre Skills measured · 12 March 2026 DP-800 exam objectives Three domains, skills measured as of 12 March 2026 on the official skills outline . Every domain below lists Microsoft's own skill groups verbatim, so you always know which domain you're being tested on and where your weak spots cluster. Data skill map Design and develop database solutions Published weight 35–40% 146 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Design topics Design and implement database objects Implement programmability objects Write advanced T-SQL code Design and implement SQL solutions by using AI-assisted tools Tests matching a specialised table type or T-SQL feature to a stated schema or query requirement. Candidates reach for a scalar function out of habit when a scenario's row count actually rules it out. Learn which programmability object is the anti-pattern before assuming any working query is the right answer. Secure, optimize, and deploy database solutions Published weight 35–40% 153 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Secure topics Implement data security and compliance Optimize database performance Implement CI/CD by using SQL Database Projects Integrate SQL solutions with Azure services Matching an encryption, performance, or deployment control to a stated production requirement is the core test. Dynamic Data Masking often gets applied when a scenario actually needs Always Encrypted to hide data from a DBA. Check whether the requirement is hiding values from ordinary users or from every privileged role before answering. Implement AI capabilities in database solutions Published weight 25–30% 114 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore AI topics Design and implement models and embeddings Design and implement intelligent search Design and implement retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) Choosing a vector-search metric, index, or RAG step order that fits the described embedding pipeline is what's graded here. This domain gets under-revised relative to its weight, since it feels newer than the SQL fundamentals. Learn the RAG sequence—retrieve, augment, generate—and recognise grounding as the use of retrieved context in the augmented prompt. Common traps Where DP-800 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared DP-800 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Dynamic Data Masking hides values from ordinary users; Always Encrypted hides them from the DBA too. A requirement that administrators must not see the data points at Always Encrypted specifically, not masking. Check whether the requirement excludes a privileged role before picking a masking or encryption feature. The vector-search metric has to match how the embeddings were actually built. Cosine, Euclidean, and dot product each suit a different embedding pipeline, and picking the wrong one is the trap. Name whether the vectors are normalised before choosing a similarity metric. ANN trades recall for latency; ENN guarantees the true nearest matches at a compute cost. A requirement for guaranteed-correct results over speed points at ENN, not a tuned ANN index. Read for a stated latency or correctness priority before choosing between the two search modes. Row counts rule out a scalar UDF before you even read the rest of the question. A scenario citing millions of rows is what should point you toward a set-based rewrite. Replace a per-row scalar function with a set-based expression once the scenario names a large row count. A RAG flow follows three core steps: retrieve, augment, generate. A language-model call with no retrieval step first is missing the "R" in RAG entirely. Check the scenario names all four RAG steps in order before assuming the flow is complete. 6-week study plan Suggested DP-800 study plan Move from SQL design and programming to security, deployment and AI integration. Use the final study blocks of this six-week route for targeted review and rehearsal. Tables and indexes Compare columnstore, memory-optimised, temporal and ledger tables. Review external and graph tables. Explore JSON columns, indexes and validation functions. Database programmability Review constraints, sequences and partitioning. Compare views, functions and stored procedures. Explore triggers, parameter sniffing and recompilation. Advanced T-SQL Practise recursive and non-recursive CTEs. Use ranking, offset and aggregate window functions. Shape JSON with SQL functions. Queries and AI-assisted development Explore regex, fuzzy matching, graph and correlated queries. Practise error handling with TRY/CATCH and error statements. Review Copilot, MCP tools, instruction files and their security implications. Data security Compare Always Encrypted with and without secure enclaves. Review masking and row-level security. Configure object permissions and auditing. Identity and keys Review passwordless managed-identity access. Manage keys with Azure Key Vault. Compare authentication across SQL Server, Azure SQL and Fabric SQL. Performance diagnosis Use DMVs, Query Store and Query Performance Insight. Analyse execution plans and regressions. Review isolation levels and blocking. Deployment and integration Use SQL Database Projects and GitHub CI/CD; manage schema drift and secrets. Explore Data API Builder, Application Insights and Log Analytics. Compare change tracking, CDC and event streaming with Functions or Logic Apps. Vectors and embeddings Register external AI models from SQL. Generate embeddings and compare chunking strategies. Build vector indexes for nearest-neighbour search. Search and RAG Compare full-text, vector and hybrid search. Review reciprocal rank fusion. Build RAG calls and parse structured outputs with REST endpoints and JSON. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Balance database design with security, optimisation and deployment. Review AI-integration gaps alongside those core areas. Timed rehearsal Complete two 100-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review the reasoning behind missed answers. Plan further practice where needed.

Core study stays on-device and works offline; optional sync uses your private iCloud account. The exam What is the DP-900 exam? DP-900 is the Microsoft Certified: Azure Data Fundamentals credential — the entry-level exam for anyone working with data in the Microsoft Azure cloud. It's pitched at candidates who have basic familiarity with relational vs non-relational data and transactional vs analytical workloads, but doesn't require database-administration experience. Common audiences include data analysts about to step into Power BI work, software engineers crossing into a data role, and product/operations partners who need to discuss data architecture credibly. The exam doesn't ask you to write SQL queries from scratch or design a star schema. It expects you to recognise scenarios: Structured vs semi-structured vs unstructured data OLTP vs OLAP workloads The difference between Azure SQL Database , Azure SQL Managed Instance , and SQL Server on Azure VMs When to reach for Azure Cosmos DB , Azure Blob Storage , or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 How Microsoft Fabric's analytics surface fits with Azure Synapse Analytics Microsoft updated the DP-900 skills outline on 21 July 2026 . Every question in Azure Mastery's DP-900 bank is mapped to the current outline — no leftover questions on retired services. Read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Questions Typically 35–50; varies Duration 45 minutes (65 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $99 (≈ £77 UK) Validity Doesn't expire (Fundamentals) Format Online or test centre Skills measured · 21 July 2026 DP-900 exam objectives Four domains, with weights set by Microsoft's 21 July 2026 update. Every domain below lists Microsoft's own skill groups verbatim from the official skills outline , so you always know which domain you're being tested on and where your weak spots cluster. Data skill map Describe core data concepts Published weight 25–30% 89 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Core Data topics Describe ways to represent data Identify options for data storage Describe common data workloads Identify roles and responsibilities for data workloads Telling structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data apart, then matching a dataset to the right database type, is the core skill here. Get the OLTP vs OLAP split wrong here and every later domain gets harder to reason about. Learn the four data roles by task, not job title: database admin, data engineer, data analyst, data scientist. Identify considerations for relational data on Azure Published weight 20–25% 86 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Relational topics Describe relational concepts Describe relational Azure data services Tests choosing between Azure SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, and SQL Server on Azure VMs for a stated need. The wrong SQL option usually gets picked because it sounds similar to the right one, not because the scenario was misread. Match migration, compatibility, and management-overhead clues to exactly one of the three options before answering. Describe considerations for working with non-relational data on Azure Published weight 15–20% 68 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Non-Relational topics Describe the capabilities of Azure storage Describe the capabilities and features of Azure Cosmos DB Picking the right storage shape — Blob tier, Table storage, or a Cosmos DB API — matters more than writing a query. Candidates treat Cosmos DB's five APIs as interchangeable when each is built around a different data model. Match relationships and traversals to Gremlin, existing MongoDB code to the MongoDB API — not whichever sounds newest. Describe an analytics workload on Azure Published weight 25–30% 103 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Analytics topics Describe common elements of large-scale analytics Describe considerations for real-time data analytics Describe data visualization in Microsoft Power BI Tests warehousing concepts, Microsoft Fabric vs Synapse Analytics, ingestion, streaming, and Power BI visualisation choices. Candidates default to Fabric on every question since recent outline updates, but some scenarios still point at Synapse specifically. Read what the scenario actually asks about — ingestion, unified analytics, or a warehousing feature — before picking a service. Common traps Where DP-900 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared DP-900 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. OLTP and OLAP describe workloads, not products Candidates try to memorise which service is OLTP or OLAP, but the same service can support either depending on how it's configured. Many small transactions point to OLTP; large aggregated reads point to OLAP — the access pattern is the tell, not the service name. Read the workload description, not a product name, before deciding whether it's OLTP or OLAP. Three SQL options solve overlapping but different problems Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, and SQL Server on a VM all run SQL Server workloads, which makes them feel interchangeable. Azure SQL Database is fully managed, Managed Instance targets instance-level compatibility, and a VM hands you the whole OS. A named compatibility or control requirement in the scenario usually rules out two of the three straight away. A Cosmos DB API choice is a data-model choice, not a preference Cosmos DB's five APIs aren't styling options on one database — each commits you to a different underlying data model. Relationships and traversals point to Gremlin; existing MongoDB code points to the MongoDB API — the data shape decides it. Pick the API the data model calls for, never the one that simply sounds more modern. Microsoft Fabric and Azure Synapse Analytics aren't competitors in every question Candidates default to picking Fabric on every analytics question since it expanded in recent skills-outline updates. A Synapse pipeline or dedicated-pool feature named specifically in the scenario still rules out the default Fabric answer. Read what the scenario is actually asking — ingestion, a unified experience, or one warehousing feature — before choosing. Structured, semi-structured, and unstructured are about shape, not size Unstructured doesn't mean unimportant or small — it means the data doesn't fit a predefined schema. Video files and free text stay unstructured regardless of size, while JSON or XML count as semi-structured whatever their length. Get this classification wrong and it cascades into picking the wrong storage service for the described file type. 2-week revision plan Suggested DP-900 study plan Build a map of data concepts and Azure services in the first week. Use the second week of this route for focused revision and timed practice. Core data concepts Study the core data concepts first. Use practice questions to check understanding. Review explanations before moving on. Relational data Compare Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance. Review SQL Server on Azure VMs. Match each service to a scenario. Non-relational data Explore Cosmos DB API options. Review Azure Storage tiers. Practise selecting a suitable service. Analytics workloads Compare Microsoft Fabric and Synapse Analytics. Review Data Factory and Stream Analytics. Explore Power BI scenarios. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Review explanations for missed questions. Revisit topics you have not practised recently. Timed rehearsal Complete two 45-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review each run carefully. Record topics that need more attention. Check your progress Complete another simulator session. Look for recurring mistakes. Use the results to plan any further study. Light review Revisit your key notes. Allow time to rest. Decide whether you are ready to move ahead.
