GH-300 is the GitHub Copilot certification — an intermediate credential for developers and technical team members who already use Copilot and want to prove real, applied expertise. It's owned and maintained by GitHub but delivered through Microsoft's exam platform, and assumes GitHub fundamentals plus experience in at least one programming language. This is not a beginner exam. It validates that you can: Use GitHub Copilot responsibly Work fluently with Copilot's features across the IDE, CLI and beyond Understand how Copilot processes your data Craft effective prompts Configure the right privacy and safeguards GH-300 is applied rather than purely conceptual — it expects a working model of how Copilot fits into a real development workflow, from inline suggestions and Copilot Chat through to organization-wide policy management. It also tests the judgement around the tool: Why you must validate AI output before trusting it How prompt context is determined When duplication detection and content exclusions matter How to read the security warnings Copilot surfaces The GH-300 skills outline was last updated on 7 August 2026 . Every question in Azure Mastery's GH-300 bank is mapped to the current six-domain outline — including newer surfaces such as Plan Mode, Agent Mode, MCP, and Spaces and Spark — with no leftover questions on retired features. Treat the 100 minutes as a closed-reference recognition and judgement exercise: practise moving from a code-completion scenario to an organisation-policy scenario without stopping to search documentation. Pay particular attention to clues that distinguish personal, Business, and Enterprise plans; repository content exclusions; public-code matching; agent versus plan mode; and prompt-context sources. Those boundaries are more durable than memorising every menu label as Copilot's product surfaces evolve. GitHub's own skill-group wording appears verbatim under each domain below, taken straight from the official study guide , so you always know exactly where a weak spot sits. Developer skill map Use GitHub Copilot Responsibly Published weight 15–20% 64 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Responsible AI topics Understand responsible AI principles Validate and operate AI tools Tests why you must validate Copilot's output before trusting it in a specific scenario. Candidates treat this domain as filler and under-study it, then miss specific harm-and-mitigation scenarios. Learn to name the failure mode — biased, insecure, or simply wrong — and how a professional responds. Use GitHub Copilot Features Published weight 25–30% 102 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Features topics Use GitHub Copilot in the IDE Use GitHub Copilot CLI Use Copilot features and capabilities Manage organization-wide settings and policies Chat, the CLI, Agent Mode, Edit Mode, and MCP each fit a different task, and matching them up is the point. Whichever feature you use daily tends to get picked, even when the scenario actually needs a different one. Learn what Agent Mode hands off to sub-agents and what MCP connects outside the editor. Understand GitHub Copilot Data and Architecture Published weight 10–15% 47 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Data & Architecture topics Describe data handling and flow Understand lifecycle and limitations Tests tracing a request: how code and prompts get filtered before a model ever sees them. Candidates skip this domain as background trivia, then miss questions on why a suggestion can be wrong. Learn exactly what the proxy service does during post-processing. Apply Prompt Engineering and Context Crafting Published weight 10–15% 48 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Prompt Engineering topics Craft effective prompts Engineer prompts for performance Prompt structure and surrounding context quietly shape what Copilot actually returns. More examples don't always help — missing that a zero-shot prompt is the right call trips people up here. Learn to read chat history back to see why a reply drifted from what you meant. Improve Developer Productivity with GitHub Copilot Published weight 10–15% 46 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Productivity topics Enhance productivity and code quality Support testing and security Tests using Copilot for code generation, refactoring, documentation, and unfamiliar-codebase ramp-up. Candidates describe productivity in vague terms instead of citing a case like Copilot cutting a task from an hour to ten minutes. Learn to pair Copilot-generated tests with the edge cases a first pass typically misses. Configure Privacy, Content Exclusions, and Safeguards Published weight 10–15% 49 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Privacy & Safeguards topics Manage privacy settings and exclusions Apply safeguards and troubleshoot A described scenario needs the specific content exclusion or safeguard that actually fits it, rather than a merely plausible one. Repository-level and organisation-level exclusions get confused when both could plausibly apply. Learn where duplication-detection filtering sits relative to a content exclusion in the pipeline. Common traps Where GH-300 candidates slip Four recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared GH-300 candidates, grounded in the current study guide. Content exclusions and duplication detection solve different problems A content exclusion stops Copilot reading a file at all, while duplication detection runs after a suggestion is generated. The exam is testing whether you pick a content exclusion to stop Copilot seeing a secrets file entirely. Pick duplication detection instead whenever the concern is shipping code that matches a public repository. Agent Mode, Edit Mode, and Chat each answer a different scope of task Chat answers a question without touching files, Edit Mode changes files you've specified, and Agent Mode executes a multi-step task alone. A task's scope and autonomy level point to one specific mode, and reading that correctly is what earns the mark. Pick the mode the task actually calls for, not whichever one you happen to use most. Zero-shot and few-shot prompting are a spectrum, not a binary choice Candidates assume more examples always produce a better suggestion, but that isn't how GH-300 grades the choice. A simple, well-understood task calls for a zero-shot prompt, and recognising that is precisely the point being tested. Reach for a few-shot prompt only when it disambiguates a pattern Copilot could otherwise guess wrong. Validating Copilot's output is a named, testable skill on this exam GH-300 doesn't treat "always check the AI's work" as background advice; it names specific failure modes to catch. The exam is testing whether you can identify a plausible-looking but insecure pattern or a hallucinated API by name. GH-900 is the GitHub Foundations certification — the standard starting point for anyone who collaborates on GitHub. It's owned and maintained by GitHub but delivered through Microsoft's exam platform, and it's designed for non-developers and developers alike: project managers, technical writers, product owners, and engineers all sit it. The exam validates that you understand: Git and version control Repositories , pull requests and branches GitHub's collaboration and project-management tools Modern development practices GitHub's privacy, security, and administration features GH-900 is conceptual rather than hands-on — it doesn't ask you to write code or configure a CI pipeline from scratch. What it does expect is a clear working model of how GitHub fits together, explained clearly enough to defend in a team conversation: The GitHub Flow How a pull request links to an issue What branch protection rules enforce When to reach for GitHub Actions , Copilot , or Codespaces How forks, templates, and the open-source community work Microsoft and GitHub last updated the GH-900 study guide on 19 February 2026 , with the skills outline reworked in January 2026. Questions Count varies by sitting Duration 100 minutes Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $99 (set by GitHub) Validity Valid for 2 years Format Online or test centre Skills measured · January 2026 GH-900 exam objectives Seven domains, with weights set by GitHub's February 2026 study-guide update. Each domain below carries GitHub's own skill-group wording verbatim from the official outline , so you can see precisely which domain a topic belongs to and where the gaps are. Developer skill map Understand Git and GitHub Basics Published weight 25–30% 91 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Basics topics Version control fundamentals Working with GitHub Tests knowing Git and GitHub are different tools, not two names for the same thing. Candidates who already use GitHub daily skip revising core Git concepts and lose easy marks. Learn the GitHub Flow by walking through its actual steps in order. Work with GitHub Repositories Published weight 10–15% 46 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Repos topics Repository management A maintenance problem points to one specific file or setting, and finding it is the exercise. README or CODEOWNERS get recognised by name but not by what each one actually controls. Learn precisely what a repository's insights panel actually exposes. Collaborate Using GitHub Published weight 10–15% 49 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Collaborate topics Collaboration tools Tests choosing the specific collaboration tool a scenario describes needing. Candidates conflate issues, discussions, and pull requests since all three carry conversation. Learn precisely how a pull request links to the issue it closes. Apply Modern Development Practices Published weight 10–15% 52 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Practices topics Automation and AI tools GitHub Actions, Copilot, and Codespaces each solve a distinct task, and telling them apart matters here. Copilot tier names get used loosely without pinning down what each tier actually controls. Learn when github.dev's lighter editor beats Codespaces for a quick edit. Manage Projects with GitHub Published weight 5–10% 33 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Projects topics Project tracking and organization Tests matching a planning need to the right Projects layout: table, board, or roadmap. Candidates treat this small domain as an afterthought and lose easy, well-defined marks. Learn what project insights actually track, beyond a simple list of open items. Understand Privacy, Security, and Administration Published weight 10–15% 48 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Security topics Security and access management A described outcome traces back to one specific setting, and pinning it down is the whole question. Personal settings like 2FA get blurred with organisation-wide controls such as Enterprise Managed Users policy. Learn exactly which force-pushes and unreviewed merges branch protection actually stops. Explore the GitHub Community Published weight 5–10% 28 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Community topics Open-source engagement Why GitHub's open-source features work the way they do is the underlying question in this domain. This domain gets skipped as unimportant, and questions on Sponsors or InnerSource get missed as a result. Learn what InnerSource actually borrows from open-source collaboration habits. Common traps Where GH-900 candidates slip Three recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared GH-900 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Git and GitHub answer different questions, and GH-900 tests the boundary directly Candidates new to source control often use the two names interchangeably, and the boundary between them is what gets tested. The exam is testing whether you know Git tracks commit history offline and GitHub hosts the pull request review. Read whether a stem asks about tracking history or about hosting collaboration before answering. github.dev and Codespaces are not the same "edit in the browser" feature github.dev is a lightweight in-browser editor with no compute behind it, while Codespaces spins up a full dev container. A quick typo fix calls for github.dev; running a build calls for Codespaces, and that split is exactly what's scored. Check whether the scenario needs real compute before choosing between the two editors. A fork and a branch solve different collaboration problems A branch is a parallel line of work in the same repository; a fork is a full copy under a different account. An external contributor without write access needs a fork, not a branch, and that call is the crux of it. Check who holds write access to the original repository before choosing between the two. 2-week revision plan Suggested GH-900 study plan Build Git and GitHub foundations, then explore collaboration, administration and community. Compare Copilot plans. Review Codespaces use cases. Projects, security and community Review GitHub project management. Explore 2FA, branch protection and Enterprise Managed Users. Compare open source, Sponsors, Marketplace and InnerSource. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Review missed questions and explanations. Revisit the topics that need more practice. PL-300 is the Microsoft Certified: Power BI Data Analyst Associate exam — the credential hiring managers expect for "Power BI Developer" or "Data Analyst" roles. It validates that you can deliver actionable insights end-to-end with Power BI, from cleaning raw data through to governed dashboards. PL-300 pairs naturally with DP-900 on the analyst track. PL-300 is hands-on and tool-aware : expect scenario questions that show a Power Query step or a DAX measure and ask you to predict the result. Across the outline, you'll cover: Connecting to and cleaning data from heterogeneous sources with Power Query (M) Designing a star-schema model with DAX calculations and time intelligence Building effective visualisations — the right visual choices, drill paths, and AI visuals Operating Power BI at scale: workspaces, deployment pipelines, gateways, refresh schedules, RLS / OLS, and Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels Microsoft updated the PL-300 skills outline on 20 April 2026 . Model the data Published weight 25–30% 101 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Model topics Design and implement a data model Create model calculations by using DAX Optimize model performance Filter context, time intelligence, and picking a calculated column against a measure are what this domain checks. Visualize and analyze the data Published weight 25–30% 118 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Visualize topics Create reports Enhance reports for usability and storytelling Identify patterns and trends Tests picking the right visual, navigation feature, or AI visual for a described reporting need. Candidates default to a familiar chart type even when the scenario calls for a different visual. Match the described trend, outlier, or driver to the AI visual built for that specific job. Manage and secure Power BI Published weight 15–20% 79 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Manage topics Create and manage workspaces and assets Secure and govern Power BI items Workspace roles, deployment pipelines, and choosing row-level versus object-level security correctly are the focus here. Under-revision here leaves row-level and object-level security tangled together in governance scenarios. Remember row-level security filters rows, while object-level security hides a whole table or column. Common traps Where PL-300 candidates slip Four recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared PL-300 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Reference and Duplicate look identical, but only one keeps a live link Both queries start from an existing one, but only Reference stays linked to its source step as that step changes. Reference depends on the source query; Duplicate copies its current steps and then evolves independently. Both can still refresh their data. Trace whether the scenario needs several queries to update together before choosing Reference over Duplicate. DirectQuery changes what a measure can and can't do Switching a table to DirectQuery changes which DAX patterns work and how a calculated column behaves at query time. The exam is testing whether you know DirectQuery changes what a calculated column can do, beyond changing speed. Check the storage mode named in the scenario before assuming a calculated column behaves as it would in Import. A measure and a calculated column don't share the same context A calculated column is fixed per row at refresh, while a measure recalculates in whatever filter context a visual applies. The exam is testing whether you can tell row context apart from filter context in a DAX scenario. Pick a measure whenever the value should react to slicers, filters, or the current visual. Object-level security is not the same control as row-level security Row-level security filters which rows a user sees, while object-level security hides an entire table or column outright. The exam is testing whether you'd pick object-level security specifically to hide a whole column, the stronger control than row filtering. Reach for object-level security whenever the scenario says hide a column or table completely, not restrict rows. 6-week study plan Suggested PL-300 study plan Build from data preparation and modelling to reports, performance and security. Convert JSON or XML and build fact and dimension tables. Query design Compare reference and duplicate queries. Practise merge and append. Review Formula.Firewall and query folding. Models and DAX Design star schemas, relationships and role-playing dimensions. Compare calculated columns with measures. Practise time intelligence and USERELATIONSHIP. Choose visuals Match chart and map types to reporting needs. Review KPIs, gauges and treemaps. Compare decomposition trees and key influencers. Report interaction Configure drill-through, drill-down and bookmarks. Build tooltip pages and synced slicers. Review filters and what-if parameters. Accessible report design Explore AI visuals, Q&A and Smart Narrative. Use custom format strings, conditional formatting and themes. Review accessibility choices. Reports and performance Compare paginated and Power BI reports. Design mobile layouts. Use Performance Analyzer and DAX Studio to investigate slow models and visuals. Publish and manage Compare workspace roles, apps and direct sharing. Review deployment pipelines. Configure gateways and refresh. Secure the data Compare static and dynamic row-level security. Review object-level security and sensitivity labels. Explore Purview integration and tenant settings. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Balance revision across the domains. PL-900 is the Microsoft Certified: Power Platform Fundamentals credential — the entry-level exam for anyone building low-code business solutions with Microsoft Power Platform. It's pitched at candidates who want to understand how Power Apps , Power Automate , Copilot Studio , and Dataverse fit together to automate processes and ship apps without deep coding. Common audiences include business analysts, citizen developers and "makers", IT pros evaluating low-code, and anyone starting a Power Platform journey. The exam doesn't ask you to build a production app from scratch. It expects you to recognise scenarios: When to use a canvas vs model-driven app Cloud vs desktop flows in Power Automate What Dataverse offers over a traditional database How Copilot Studio agents use topics, knowledge sources, and channels The business value of connectors and generative AI across Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, and Azure Microsoft updated the PL-900 skills outline on 24 July 2026 — Power Pages was removed and a new Copilot Studio agents domain was added. Business solutions skill map Describe the business value of Microsoft Power Platform Published weight 5–10% 30 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Business Value topics Describe the business value of Microsoft Power Platform services Matching a described business problem to the right service — Power Apps, Power Automate, Dataverse, a connector, Power Pages, or Copilot Studio — is what this domain actually asks. This short domain gets skimmed, then a scenario naming Power Pages or Copilot Studio instead of Power Apps causes a blank. Write one clear value sentence per service before moving on; every later domain assumes you already know this split. Manage the Microsoft Power Platform environment Published weight 20–25% 76 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Environment topics Describe Microsoft Dataverse Describe Microsoft Power Platform administration and governance This domain splits in two: Dataverse's data model and business logic, then the governance layer of environments and ALM. Dataverse's tables and forms get studied closely while governance topics like pipelines get skipped, leaving people underprepared. Give environments, security roles, and Power Platform pipelines the same revision time as Dataverse's tables and views. Demonstrate the capabilities of Power Apps Published weight 20–25% 76 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Power Apps topics Describe Power Apps capabilities and use cases Describe how to build basic apps by using Power Apps This domain tests choosing between canvas apps, model-driven apps, the Plan designer, and code apps for a stated need. Candidates default to canvas apps for everything, missing scenarios where a data-heavy process actually points to model-driven. Name the app type first, then check why the other three options would suit the scenario worse. Demonstrate the capabilities of Power Automate Published weight 20–25% 70 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Power Automate topics Describe Power Automate use cases and capabilities Describe how to build basic flows by using Power Automate This domain tests telling cloud flows and desktop flows apart, plus matching a connector to a described automation task. Candidates assume any repetitive task suits a cloud flow, even when the scenario describes an old app with no API. Check whether the scenario's target system is reachable through a connector before choosing cloud over desktop flow. Describe features and capabilities of agents in Microsoft Copilot Studio Published weight 20–25% 76 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Agents topics Describe how to build agents in Copilot Studio Describe how to manage agents in Copilot Studio Separating an agent's topics, knowledge sources, and tools, plus knowing how Microsoft Agent 365 manages published agents, is the focus here. This domain gets under-revised since it only joined the outline in the July 2026 refresh, and half its questions get missed as a result. Decide which of topics, knowledge sources, or tools a described capability belongs to before you touch practice questions. Common traps Where PL-900 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared PL-900 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Canvas apps and model-driven apps solve different design problems Both build apps inside Power Apps, so candidates assume the choice between them is just a style preference. A bespoke, highly visual layout points to canvas; a data-heavy process built around existing tables points to model-driven. Tie your answer to what drives the scenario: free-form design points to canvas, standard forms and views point to model-driven. A cloud flow and a desktop flow automate different kinds of system Candidates treat cloud and desktop flows as interchangeable automation tools rather than two options built for very different targets. Desktop flows exist specifically for legacy or local apps that have no connector available for a cloud flow to use. Spot a scenario describing an old desktop application with no API, then pick desktop flow over cloud flow. Topics, knowledge sources, and tools are three separate parts of an agent These Copilot Studio building blocks get tested against each other constantly, and candidates blur them into one idea. Topics define the conversation path; knowledge sources ground the agent's answers in your own content instead. Read the verb in the scenario: answering from a document is knowledge sources, not a topic or a tool. Dataverse bundles more than a hosted database Candidates describe Dataverse as simply a database Microsoft hosts, missing the governance and logic layers built on top. Business logic, security roles, and low-code tooling all sit on top of Dataverse's stored tables, not beside them. Name a governance feature, such as security roles or business rules, whenever a question contrasts Dataverse with a plain database. Creating an environment is not the same task as deploying through one Candidates conflate setting up an environment with moving a solution between environments using Power Platform pipelines. Environment administration and the pipelines that carry solutions between environments are tested as two separate governance topics. Treat environments and pipelines as two governance topics and revise each with its own practice questions. 2-week revision plan Suggested PL-900 study plan Build a map of Power Platform services in the first week. Use the second week for focused revision and timed practice, adjusting the pace to your experience. Business value and environments Review Power Platform business value. Compare Dataverse with a traditional database. Explore environments, security and ALM pipelines. Power Apps Compare canvas, model-driven and code apps. Explore the Plan designer and AI-assisted app building. Practise choosing an app type for a scenario. Power Automate Compare cloud and desktop flows. Review connector triggers and actions. Explore approval, Teams, Outlook and SharePoint scenarios. Copilot Studio agents Review topics and knowledge sources. Explore MCP tools and agent flows. Compare channels and review Microsoft Agent 365. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Review explanations for missed questions. Revisit topics you have not practised recently. entries.summary: Which Microsoft certification exams retired in 2026, when, and which current exam replaced each one — AI-900, AI-102, DP-100, AZ-204, and AZ-500.
entries.text: Retired exams Retired Microsoft exams and what replaced them Microsoft retires a certification exam when the underlying role or technology has moved on, replacing it with an exam that reflects the job as it's actually done today. A credential you already earned stays valid and stays on your transcript regardless, and Azure Mastery keeps each retired exam's question bank in the app as reference material for anyone who passed — or bought — it before retirement. At a glance The retired exams and their successors Retirement dates come from Microsoft's own published schedule; successor routes match the ones linked from each exam's own page. Exam Name Retired on Successor Credential status AI-900 Microsoft Azure AI Fundamentals 30 June 2026 AI-901 Earned credential stays on transcript AI-102 Microsoft Azure AI Engineer Associate 30 June 2026 AI-103 Earned credential stays on transcript DP-100 Designing and Implementing a Data Science Solution on Azure 1 June 2026 AI-300 Earned credential stays on transcript AZ-204 Azure Developer Associate 31 July 2026 AI-200 Earned credential stays on transcript AZ-500 Microsoft Azure Security Engineer 31 August 2026 SC-500 Bookable until retirement; credential then stays on transcript AI-900 → AI-901 AI-900 → AI-901 AI-900 retired on 30 June 2026. Its direct successor is AI-901 (Microsoft Azure AI Fundamentals). The core ideas carry over: AI and ML terminology, responsible AI principles, and a working sense of computer vision and natural language workloads. AI-901 weights implementation far more heavily, with more than half the exam on building solutions with Microsoft Foundry rather than just recognising Azure AI services. See how to pass AI-901 for a full domain breakdown and study plan. AI-102 → AI-103 AI-102 → AI-103 AI-102 retired on 30 June 2026. Its direct successor is AI-103 (Microsoft Azure AI App & Agent Developer Associate). Most of AI-102's domain structure survives unchanged: planning and managing an AI solution, computer vision, and generative AI all remain. Two domains were renamed: AI-102's separate agentic-solution domain folded into "implement generative AI and agentic solutions", and its natural-language and knowledge-mining objectives now sit under "text analysis" and "information extraction". DP-100 → AI-300 DP-100 → AI-300 DP-100 retired on 1 June 2026. Microsoft's current guidance treats AI-300 (Microsoft ML Operations Engineer) as the closest replacement, though the two aren't a like-for-like swap. DP-100 tested designing, preparing and training models; AI-300 assumes that skill and tests operating them at scale instead, through MLOps pipelines, model lifecycle management, and generative-AI operations. Candidates who mostly used DP-100 for training and deploying models will find AI-300's model-lifecycle domain the closest overlap. DP-100's data-exploration and experimentation content has no direct equivalent in AI-300. AZ-204 → AI-200 AZ-204 → AI-200 AZ-204 retired on 31 July 2026. Its listed successor is AI-200 (Azure AI Cloud Developer). AI-200 reuses a similar domain shape to AZ-204 (compute, storage, security and monitoring) applied specifically to AI workloads instead of general Azure development. A developer who studied AZ-204's compute, storage and security domains already recognises AI-200's structure. What changes is mostly which services those domains cover: AI-powered compute hosts, vector-enabled storage, and AI-specific identity and monitoring. AZ-500 → SC-500 AZ-500 → SC-500 AZ-500 retired on 31 August 2026, the last of the five exams on this page to close. Its successor is SC-500 (Cloud and AI Security Engineer). SC-500 keeps AZ-500's structure almost intact: identity and access, storage/database/network security, and security-posture management all carry over directly. The one substantive addition is AI-workload security, folded into SC-500's compute domain, reflecting the new class of resources security engineers now have to protect.

Core study stays on-device and works offline; optional sync uses your private iCloud account. The exam What is the SC-100 exam? SC-100 is the exam for the Microsoft Certified: Cybersecurity Architect Expert credential — the most senior security cert in Microsoft's track. It's the credential hiring managers expect for "Cybersecurity Architect", "Lead Security Engineer", or "Cloud Security Architect" roles. Passing SC-100 alone doesn't award the certification: Microsoft also requires one of three active Associate-level credentials — Identity and Access Administrator Associate (SC-300), Security Operations Analyst Associate (SC-200), or Cloud and AI Security Engineer Associate (SC-500). Microsoft replaced the retired AZ-500 route with SC-500 in the current prerequisite list. You can take SC-100 before earning the Associate credential, but the expert certification is awarded only after both requirements are active on your profile. The prerequisite is the active Associate credential, not merely a pass on its exam. SC-100 is design-oriented and trade-off-heavy . Unlike Associate exams that test individual-service knowledge, it tests architectural reasoning: picking the right strategy under real-world constraints. It validates that you can: Apply the Microsoft Cybersecurity Reference Architecture (MCRA) Design a Zero Trust strategy and a ransomware-resilience stance Build SecOps strategies around Microsoft Sentinel and Defender XDR Design identity strategies in Microsoft Entra — Conditional Access, PIM, Identity Governance Design infrastructure security spanning endpoints, servers, containers, networks, and keys Design application and data security, including DevSecOps Expect scenario questions where multiple answers could work; the right one is whichever best satisfies the stated constraints. Architectural questions often turn on where a control operates: tenant, management plane, workload edge, or external attack surface. Sketch the trust boundary and ownership model before comparing products; a technically capable service can still be wrong when it leaves the required control plane or evidence source untouched. Microsoft updated the SC-100 skills outline on 28 July 2026 . Every question in Azure Mastery's SC-100 bank is mapped to the current outline — no leftover questions on retired services. Read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Questions 40–60 multiple choice Duration 120 minutes (140 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $165 (≈ £128 UK) Validity Renew annually (Expert) Format Online or test centre Skills measured · 28 July 2026 SC-100 exam objectives SC-100 has four domains, and Microsoft's 28 July 2026 refresh set the weights. Each summary below follows the official skills outline ; the counts are the questions in the app tagged to that domain. Security skill map Design solutions that align with security best practices and priorities Published weight 20–25% 98 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Best Practices topics Design a resiliency strategy for ransomware and other attacks based on Microsoft Security Best Practices Design solutions that align with the Microsoft Cybersecurity Reference Architectures (MCRA) and Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB) Design solutions that align with the Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure (CAF) and the Azure Well-Architected Framework This domain tests setting direction: ransomware resilience, MCRA and MCSB alignment, and CAF or WAF governance recommendations. Candidates who only studied Associate-level configuration struggle here, since the exam wants a recommended strategy, not a setting. Practise stating which framework, MCRA, MCSB, or CAF, a described requirement calls for before naming any product. Design security operations, identity, and compliance capabilities Published weight 25–30% 139 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore SecOps topics Design solutions for security operations Design solutions for identity and access management Design solutions for securing privileged access Design solutions for regulatory compliance This domain spans the most products: SecOps design with Sentinel and Defender XDR, identity strategy, privileged access, and compliance. Legacy admin-tiering language often replaces the enterprise access model the exam now expects. Learn the enterprise access model's three planes before practising any privileged-access scenario in this domain. Design security solutions for infrastructure Published weight 25–30% 127 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Infrastructure topics Design solutions for security posture management in hybrid and multicloud environments Specify requirements for securing server and client endpoints Specify requirements for securing SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS services Evaluate solutions for network security and Security Service Edge (SSE) This domain tests specifying requirements across posture management, endpoints, SaaS/PaaS/IaaS, and Security Service Edge. Candidates confuse Defender for Cloud's posture management with Sentinel's active threat response, though the exam treats them separately. Keep posture management and active response as two separate domains in your head; scenarios rarely mix them. Design security solutions for applications and data Published weight 20–25% 108 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Apps & Data topics Evaluate solutions for securing Microsoft 365 Design solutions for securing applications Design solutions for securing an organization's data Securing Microsoft 365 workloads, application threat modelling, and data protection including AI workloads all sit in this domain. The newer requirement to evaluate data-security controls in Microsoft Copilot for Microsoft 365 gets under-revised most often. Add Copilot data-security evaluation to your revision list; it's a recent addition many candidates miss. Common traps Where SC-100 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared SC-100 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Zero Trust is an architecture, not a single control Candidates who deployed MFA or network segmentation sometimes treat either one alone as doing Zero Trust. A single strong control, deployed harder, still reads as incomplete if the other pillars stay silent. Build a Zero Trust answer that touches at least two pillars before you commit to a single-control fix. MCRA, MCSB, and CAF or WAF answer different questions Candidates reach for whichever framework name they remember best rather than the one the scenario actually calls for. MCRA is a reference architecture; MCSB provides prescriptive security recommendations; CAF and WAF guide adoption and workload design. A posture-management tool can assess an environment against MCSB, but the benchmark itself does not perform the measurement. The enterprise access model has replaced legacy admin tiering Candidates who studied older AD-centric tiering default to Tier 0, 1, 2 language on a privileged-access scenario. Reasoning in terms of the control, management, and data-or-workload planes now replaces tier numbers entirely. Retire Tier 0/1/2 language from your answers and reason in terms of the three enterprise access model planes. Posture management and active response are different domains Defender for Cloud appearing in a scenario doesn't automatically make the question about security operations. A SOAR or incident-response design belongs in security operations, whatever product name the scenario mentions. Ask whether the scenario wants a measurement of risk or a response to an active threat before choosing a domain. The prerequisite gates the certification, not the exam booking Candidates researching "can I take SC-100 first" often assume the prerequisite blocks registration itself. Content readiness is what SC-100 grades; the prerequisite sits outside the exam, as a separate certification-award policy. Book SC-100 whenever you're ready on content, and separately earn an active SC-200, SC-300, or SC-500 prerequisite certification. 6-week study plan Suggested SC-100 study plan Practise security architecture decisions across strategy, infrastructure, applications and data. Use these six weeks of study blocks to build your trade-off reasoning, then rehearse. Security architecture frameworks Review the Microsoft Cybersecurity Reference Architecture. Explore the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark. Review the Cloud Adoption Framework security baseline. Zero Trust and resilience Design Zero Trust across identities, endpoints and networks. Extend the strategy to applications and data. Review ransomware resilience and recovery. Compliance and risk Review compliance requirements and their design implications. Consider sovereign-cloud constraints. Compare risk-assessment approaches. Security operations strategy Design SecOps with Sentinel and Defender XDR. Plan Entra access controls and identity governance. Review Purview compliance strategy. Endpoint and server strategy Compare Defender for Endpoint and Defender for Servers. Review secure baselines. Plan hybrid and multi-cloud coverage with Azure Arc. Network security strategy Design segmentation and perimeter protection. Plan private connectivity. Review Defender for Cloud network maps. Keys and secure access Compare Key Vault, customer-managed keys and HSMs. Plan secret management. Review Bastion and just-in-time VM access. Container security Review Defender for Containers and AKS hardening. Plan image scanning. Consider software supply-chain protection. Application security strategy Review secure development lifecycle choices. Plan DevSecOps and supply-chain security. Practise threat modelling. Data security strategy Review Purview Information Protection and labels. Compare encryption choices for SQL, Cosmos DB and Storage. Consider data residency. Practise trade-off reasoning Use Focus Weak Spots to revisit gaps. Re-read scenarios you missed. Explain why each alternative is unsuitable. Timed rehearsal Complete two 120-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review the reasoning behind missed answers. Plan further practice where needed.

Questions 40–60 multiple choice Duration 100 minutes (120 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $165 (≈ £128 UK) Validity Renew annually (Associate) Format Online or test centre Skills measured · 28 July 2026 SC-200 exam objectives SC-200 has three domains, weighted by Microsoft's 28 July 2026 update. Each summary below follows the official skills outline ; the counts are the questions in the app tagged to that domain. Security skill map Manage a security operations environment Published weight 40–45% 162 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore SecOps topics Configure automation for Microsoft Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel Configure the Microsoft Sentinel SIEM and platform Ingest data into the Microsoft Sentinel SIEM and platform Configure detections This domain tests configuring Sentinel end-to-end and picking the right ingestion connector for a described log source. Candidates memorise connector names but mix up which topology, AMA, WEF, or Syslog/CEF, actually fits a given source. Match a described source and network topology to its one correct connector before touching other domain content. Respond to security incidents Published weight 35–40% 132 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Incidents topics Respond to alerts and incidents in Microsoft Defender XDR Respond to alerts and incidents in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Investigate Microsoft 365 activities to identify threats Investigating and remediating across the whole Defender XDR surface, now including agentic AI tooling, is the real focus here. Case management and the evidence graph often get treated as one feature, though one tracks tasks and the other traces movement. Reach for the attack-story graph specifically whenever a scenario asks how an attack actually moved. Perform threat hunting Published weight 20–25% 80 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Hunt topics Detect threats by using Microsoft Defender XDR Detect threats by using the Microsoft Sentinel platform This domain is the most KQL-heavy: picking the right table and writing a query that actually returns results. Syntactically correct KQL against the wrong table returns an empty result that's hard to explain. Identify the correct table for a described signal before writing any KQL; that choice is itself assessed. Common traps Where SC-200 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared SC-200 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Defender for Cloud measures posture; Defender XDR handles response Defender for Cloud surfacing an alert doesn't make the follow-up question a posture-management one. Use Defender XDR for cross-product incident investigation; use Defender for Cloud for cloud posture and workload-protection findings, with integrations connecting the two workflows. Treat Defender for Cloud as where risk is measured and Defender XDR as where an active incident gets handled. Analytics rules, automation rules, and playbooks are three separate layers Candidates reach for an analytics rule when a scenario actually needs automated remediation of an existing incident. An analytics rule detects, an automation rule routes, and only a playbook actually remediates. Pick a playbook whenever the scenario names a remediation action like isolating a device or disabling an account. The right data connector depends on the source, not habit AMA, WEF, and Syslog/CEF connectors all bring log data into Sentinel, so candidates default to whichever they know best. Matching a described source and topology to its one purpose-built connector is what earns the mark here. Pick WEF for centralised on-premises forwarding and CEF/Syslog for third-party appliances, not whichever connector feels familiar. KQL table choice changes what a query can even see Correct KQL syntax against the wrong table still returns an empty or misleading result. Naming the table that actually holds the described telemetry is itself a scored step, before any query gets written. Name the correct table first; treat that identification as a scored step, not a formality before the real answer. Case management tracks the incident; the graph explains it Candidates reach for case management when a scenario is actually asking how an attack moved between hosts. A lateral-movement question calls for the evidence and attack-story graph, or Sentinel Graph, not the case list. Save case management for tracking tasks and status; use the graph whenever the question is about how an attack spread. 6-week study plan Suggested SC-200 study plan Build the SecOps environment, practise incident response, then develop your threat-hunting skills. Explore user and entity behaviour analytics where supported. Automate incident handling Configure automation rules and Logic App playbooks. Practise triage, enrichment and response actions. Build workbooks and dashboards. Defender for Cloud Review Secure Score and regulatory compliance. Compare workload protection plans. Explore JIT access, recommendations and exemptions. Endpoint response Review live response and automated investigation. Practise response actions. Explore device groups and attack-surface reduction. Identity threats Review lateral movement and golden-ticket detection. Explore identity scoring. Understand sensors and connectors. Email and collaboration threats Review anti-phishing and zero-hour auto purge. Compare Safe Links and Safe Attachments. Explore attack-simulation training. Cloud apps and XDR Review Cloud Apps anomaly detection and governance actions. Use the XDR attack-story view and evidence graph. Practise kill-chain analysis. KQL practice Review joins, parsing and time windows. Use summarise, project and extend. Interpret KQL snippets in scenarios. Threat hunting Explore Sentinel queries, bookmarks and livestream sessions. Review custom detections and Defender XDR advanced hunting. Map findings to MITRE ATT&CK. Study offline with on-device processing, or enable private iCloud sync to carry your progress between devices. The exam What is the SC-300 exam? SC-300 is the Microsoft Certified: Identity and Access Administrator Associate exam — the credential hiring managers expect when posting "Identity Administrator", "IAM Engineer", "Microsoft Entra Administrator", or "Identity and Access Manager" roles. SC-300 covers the day-to-day of operating Microsoft Entra ID at scale — identities, authentication, Conditional Access, workload identities, and identity governance. It pairs with SC-900 on the way in, and is one of the prereqs for SC-100 (Cybersecurity Architect Expert) . SC-300 is hands-on and Entra-deep . It validates that you can: Implement and manage user identities — cloud-only, hybrid, guest Configure authentication: passwordless, MFA, password protection, SSPR Design and operate Conditional Access and Microsoft Entra ID Protection Plan workload identities — service principals, managed identities, app registrations, OAuth flows, app proxy Run identity governance via entitlement management, access reviews, and Privileged Identity Management (PIM) Expect scenario questions that show you a Conditional Access policy JSON or an access-package configuration and ask what you'd change. Microsoft updated the SC-300 skills outline on 27 April 2026 . Every question in Azure Mastery's SC-300 bank is mapped to the current outline — no leftover questions on retired services. Read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Questions 40–60 multiple choice Duration 100 minutes (120 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $165 (≈ £128 UK) Validity Renew annually (Associate) Format Online or test centre Skills measured · 27 April 2026 SC-300 exam objectives SC-300 spans four domains, weighted by Microsoft's 27 April 2026 update. Each summary below follows the official skills outline ; the counts are the questions in the app tagged to that domain. Security skill map Implement and manage user identities Published weight 20–25% 106 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Identities topics Configure and manage a Microsoft Entra tenant Create, configure, and manage Microsoft Entra identities Implement and manage identities for external users and tenants Implement and manage hybrid identity This domain tests picking the correct hybrid-identity method, PHS, PTA, or federation, for a stated resilience requirement. Candidates know all three sync methods exist but default to whichever they've used before, not the one the scenario needs. Match PHS to on-premises-outage resilience and PTA to real-time on-premises validation before answering any hybrid-identity question. Implement authentication and access management Published weight 25–30% 127 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Access topics Plan, implement, and manage Microsoft Entra user authentication Plan, implement, and manage Microsoft Entra Conditional Access Manage risk by using Microsoft Entra ID Protection Implement Global Secure Access This domain covers the widest surface: authentication methods, the full Conditional Access lifecycle, ID Protection, and Global Secure Access. Security defaults and Conditional Access policies don't layer; turning on the custom policy set means switching security defaults off. Confirm a tenant runs security defaults or custom Conditional Access, never both, before reasoning about a described policy. Plan and implement workload identities Published weight 20–25% 107 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Workload topics Plan and implement identities for applications and Azure workloads Plan, implement, and monitor the integration of enterprise applications Plan and implement app registrations Manage and monitor app access by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps Choosing between managed identities, service principals, and app registrations for an application scenario is the core test here. Candidates from a pure end-user background underestimate this domain and confuse a managed identity with a manually created service principal. Pick a managed identity whenever a scenario wants to avoid managing secrets for an Azure-hosted workload. Plan and automate identity governance Published weight 20–25% 108 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Governance topics Plan and implement entitlement management in Microsoft Entra Plan, implement, and manage access reviews in Microsoft Entra Plan and implement privileged access Monitor identity activity by using logs, workbooks, and reports This domain tests the full governance lifecycle: entitlement management, access reviews, PIM, and identity activity monitoring. PIM eligibility often gets treated as an active assignment, though eligibility alone grants no standing access. Remember an eligible PIM assignment needs activation before permissions apply; only an active assignment applies them immediately. Operational practice Run an SC-300 identity-control lab loop Use a disposable development tenant to practise the evidence trail behind an identity decision. The useful skill is not memorising a portal path; it is proving which identity, policy, permission, and governance object produced the result. 1. Separate attribute definition from assignment Create a small custom security attribute set, define one constrained attribute, and assign a permitted value to a test user. Record which role can manage the definition and which role can assign values within that attribute set. Before saving, identify the schema choices that cannot be changed later; then remove the test assignment and note what remains in the directory. 2. Explain a Conditional Access result from evidence Build a report-only policy, predict its outcome with What If, and then make one controlled test sign-in. Capture the user, target resource, conditions, and expected grant controls before the sign-in so the result can be compared with the prediction. Use the sign-in record's Conditional Access details, request ID, and policy evaluation rather than guessing from the final error message. 3. Trace risky OAuth consent to a response Review an app's requested permissions, publisher details, consent activity, and usage before deciding whether its access is expected. Write an app-policy filter that isolates the behaviour you want to monitor, then distinguish the alert condition from the action taken after investigation. Practise choosing among monitoring, revoking consent, and banning an app; each response needs evidence proportional to its impact. 4. Model an external access request end to end Add a test connected organization, choose its identity sources and sponsors, and include it in an access-package policy. Keep the connected organization, catalog, access package, and assignment policy as separate objects in your notes. Compare proposed and configured connected organizations, then verify what the external requester sees and which approval evidence the sponsor receives. Finish each exercise with a five-column evidence sheet: expected identity, target resource, predicted control, observed log, and cleanup action. That habit turns a vague identity scenario into an auditable chain you can reason through under exam pressure. Common traps Where SC-300 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared SC-300 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. PHS, PTA, and federation behave differently during an on-premises outage Candidates know the three hybrid-identity methods by name but don't connect each one to a specific failure mode. PHS keeps sign-in working through an on-premises outage; PTA fails closed the moment its on-premises agent goes dark. Pick PHS whenever a scenario specifically asks for resilience against an on-premises infrastructure outage. Security defaults and Conditional Access can't run together Candidates assume the two layer on top of each other rather than being mutually exclusive. Turning on any Conditional Access policy requires switching security defaults off first, not layering the two. Recognise that a tenant with custom Conditional Access policies has already left security defaults behind. PIM eligibility grants no access until it's activated Candidates treat an eligible assignment as equivalent to an active one with a shorter duration. An eligible assignment needs activation, often through approval, before a single permission actually applies. Pick eligible assignment plus activation requirements whenever a scenario asks for just-in-time access to a sensitive role. A managed identity and a service principal solve the same problem differently Both are application identities, so candidates treat them as interchangeable terms for the same thing. Microsoft creates and rotates a managed identity's credentials automatically; a service principal leaves that work to you. Pick a managed identity whenever a scenario wants to avoid managing secrets or certificates for an Azure-hosted workload. A catalog and an access package are two different governance objects Candidates use the two entitlement-management terms interchangeably when they describe different layers of the same feature. A catalog groups resources available for request; a package is the specific bundle a user actually receives. Configure the catalog first whenever a scenario asks you to add a new resource type available for request. 6-week study plan Suggested SC-300 study plan Build from user identities and authentication to application access and governance. Follow these six weeks of study blocks, then review your progress with timed practice. Users, groups and tenants Review tenant settings and identity types. Practise bulk operations. Explore dynamic groups and group writeback. Hybrid and external identities Compare Connect Sync, cloud sync, PHS, PTA and federation. Review SSPR registration and B2B collaboration. Explore lifecycle workflows. Authentication methods Compare FIDO2, Windows Hello and Authenticator. Review MFA, password protection and smart lockout. Distinguish security defaults from Conditional Access. Conditional Access Plan named locations and sign-in risk controls. Compare session controls and app-enforced restrictions. Review Defender for Cloud Apps integration. Identity Protection Investigate risky users. Review risky sign-ins. Compare remediation policies and thresholds. Workload identities Compare service principals and managed identities. Distinguish system-assigned and user-assigned identities. Review federated credentials. App registrations and consent Review OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect flows. Compare application and delegated permissions. Explore admin-consent workflows. Application access Review Application Proxy. Compare SAML and SSO for legacy and gallery apps. Explore Conditional Access for workload identities. Entitlement management Create access packages and catalogs. Review assignment and lifecycle policies. Plan separation of duties. Access reviews and privileges Review access to groups, apps and roles. Practise PIM eligibility, activation and approvals. Compare role reviews and access-review workflows. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Revisit authentication and access-management scenarios. Review explanations for recurring mistakes. Timed rehearsal Complete two 100-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review each run carefully. Plan further practice where needed.

Every domain below lists Microsoft's own skill groups verbatim from the official skills outline , so you always know which domain you're being tested on and where your weak spots cluster. Security skill map Manage identity, access, and governance Published weight 20–25% 110 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Identity topics Secure access to resources by using Microsoft Entra ID Secure secrets and keys by using Azure Key Vault Implement governance to enforce security and regulatory compliance Covers PIM's eligible-vs-active roles, Conditional Access session controls, and managed identities replacing stored secrets. Governance often gets treated as separate from identity, but RBAC hygiene and policy enforcement sit in this same domain. Prove a policy actually blocks what it claims — don't assume a policy existing means it's enforcing anything. Secure storage, databases, and networking Published weight 25–30% 116 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Data & Network topics Implement security for storage accounts Implement security for databases Implement security for Azure network services The largest domain: Defender for Storage, Azure SQL auditing, and networking controls across NSGs, endpoints, and firewalls. Candidates default to encryption-at-rest for storage questions when the scenario is really testing Defender threat protection. Practise reading Azure Firewall and Network Watcher output to confirm a rule does what a scenario claims. Secure compute Published weight 20–25% 113 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Compute topics Implement security for AI Implement security for servers and virtual machines (VMs) Implement security for application platform services Splits three ways: AI security with no AZ-500 equivalent, server hardening, and application-platform controls across hosting models. Matching a control to its hosting model is the trap — a Container Apps control won't fix a Functions app. New to this exam: Purview DSPM, Entra Agent ID, and Defender for AI Services guardrails need dedicated study. Manage and monitor security posture Published weight 20–25% 113 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Posture topics Manage security posture by using Defender for Cloud Implement activity and event collection in Microsoft Sentinel Implement Microsoft Security Copilot The operational half: proving Defender for Cloud and Sentinel controls actually work, beyond simply configuring them. Candidates guess at Sentinel ingestion mechanics instead of matching a data source to its actual pipeline. Practise picking the right ingestion path — connector, CEF, or a custom log table — for a named data source. Common traps Where SC-500 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared SC-500 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Treating SC-500 as AZ-500 with a new name Candidates study only AZ-500 material and consistently underperform on SC-500's dedicated AI-security slice. Purview DSPM, Entra Agent ID, and Foundry guardrails carry no AZ-500 equivalent, and the exam weights them accordingly. Add AI-security topics to your plan even if you already hold AZ-500 — don't assume the overlap is complete. Defender for Storage vs a storage firewall rule Candidates mix up a network-perimeter control with a threat-detection control inside the same storage domain. A firewall rule blocks traffic before authentication; Defender for Storage detects suspicious activity after access has already happened. For a scenario describing an attack already underway, pick the detection answer, not the network-perimeter one. Treating Entra Agent ID like a normal app registration Candidates default to classic Conditional Access or PIM patterns for scenarios that actually describe an autonomous agent. Entra Agent ID governs autonomous agents specifically, distinct from human sign-ins and conventional service principals. Look for an agent chaining actions across systems as the cue to reach for Agent ID's own controls. Defender CSPM vs the free foundational tier Candidates assume the free foundational tier already covers attack-path analysis and multicloud governance. Attack-path analysis and agentless scanning both sit behind the paid CSPM layer, not the free foundational tier. Match multicloud coverage or governance-at-scale requirements to CSPM, not the free tier. Assuming every Sentinel source lands the same way Candidates pick the wrong ingestion mechanism or invent a custom table where a built-in one already exists. Syslog, Windows events, and genuinely custom sources each need a different ingestion path, and mixing them up is the common miss. Check for an existing built-in table like CommonSecurityLog before assuming a source needs a custom one. 6-week study plan Suggested SC-500 study plan Move from identity and governance to workload protection, AI security and operations. Use the final blocks of this six-week route for focused review and timed practice. Identity and access Compare authentication methods, MFA and passwordless access. Review Conditional Access locations, risk and sessions. Practise PIM eligibility, activation and access reviews. Application identities and keys Review enterprise apps, registrations and OAuth consent. Use managed identities for Azure resources. Configure Key Vault access, networking and protection. Governance Review built-in and custom Azure Policy definitions. Compare built-in and custom RBAC roles. Remediate excessive permissions and apply resource locks. Compliance and recovery controls Review compliance in Defender for Cloud. Explore Azure Backup security. Apply security controls through infrastructure as code. Storage and databases Secure storage accounts, firewalls and access policies. Review Defender for Storage. Explore SQL security, auditing and Defender for Databases. Network security Review NSGs, ASGs, Virtual Network Manager and Virtual WAN. Compare VPN, Entra Private Access, Private Link and private endpoints. Explore Azure Firewall and Network Watcher. Compute and app platforms Review disk encryption, Bastion, JIT access, Arc and trusted launch controls. Explore Defender for Servers and container-platform protection. Review Functions, Logic Apps, App Service, WAF and API Management security. AI security Review Purview DSPM for Copilot. Explore Entra Agent ID controls and Defender XDR blast-radius analysis. Review AI Gateway, Defender for AI and Foundry agent guardrails. Security posture Review Defender CSPM, compliance and workload protection. Connect AWS and GCP environments. Explore vulnerability management and external attack-surface management. Sentinel and Security Copilot Configure workspaces, roles and Content Hub solutions. Review connectors, event collection and data collection rules. Explore automation rules, playbooks and Security Copilot plugins or agents. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Revisit storage, database and networking decisions. Review explanations for missed scenarios. Timed rehearsal Complete two 100-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review each run carefully. Use the results to plan further study.

Azure Mastery uses on-device AI to predict your readiness score, build a personalised study plan, and surface topics you're forgetting. Core study stays on-device and works offline; optional sync uses your private iCloud account. The exam What is the SC-900 exam? SC-900 is the Microsoft Certified: Security, Compliance, and Identity Fundamentals credential — the entry-level exam for anyone working with (or making decisions about) Microsoft's security stack across both Azure and Microsoft 365. It's pitched at business stakeholders, new and existing IT professionals, and students who want a credible foundation in Microsoft SCI solutions. Common audiences include security analysts about to step into SC-200 , identity administrators heading toward SC-300 , and architects on the path to SC-100 (Cybersecurity Architect Expert) . The exam doesn't ask you to configure a Conditional Access policy or write a KQL query. It expects you to recognise scenarios across the SCI surface: The shared responsibility model , defence-in-depth , and Zero Trust Encryption vs hashing , and identity vs authentication vs authorization The role of Microsoft Entra ID and its identity types The capabilities of Microsoft Defender products and Microsoft Sentinel Microsoft's compliance solutions, including Microsoft Purview Microsoft updated the SC-900 skills outline on 28 July 2026 . Every question in Azure Mastery's SC-900 bank is mapped to the current outline — no leftover questions on retired services. Read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Questions Typically 35–50; varies Duration 45 minutes (65 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 Cost USD $99 (≈ £77 UK) Validity Doesn't expire (Fundamentals) Format Online or test centre Skills measured · 28 July 2026 SC-900 exam objectives Four domains, with weights set by Microsoft's 28 July 2026 update. Every domain below lists Microsoft's own skill groups verbatim from the official skills outline , so you always know which domain you're being tested on and where your weak spots cluster. Security skill map Describe the concepts of security, compliance, and identity Published weight 10–15% 51 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Concepts topics Describe security and compliance concepts Define identity concepts This domain sets the vocabulary every later domain assumes: shared responsibility, defence-in-depth, Zero Trust, and identity as the perimeter. Authentication and authorization get confused here, and that confusion carries into every Entra question that follows. Lock down authentication versus authorization before moving on; the exam keeps testing that one distinction. Describe the capabilities of Microsoft Entra Published weight 25–30% 112 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Entra topics Describe function and identity types of Microsoft Entra ID Describe authentication capabilities of Microsoft Entra ID Describe access management capabilities of Microsoft Entra ID Describe identity protection and governance capabilities of Microsoft Entra This domain tests sorting a described capability into one of four sub-areas: identity types, authentication, access management, or governance. Candidates know Conditional Access and Privileged Identity Management by name but mix up which sub-area each belongs to. Name the sub-area first, then the specific Entra feature; the exam rewards that ordering. Describe the capabilities of Microsoft security solutions Published weight 35–40% 150 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Security topics Describe core infrastructure security services in Azure Describe security management capabilities of Azure Describe capabilities of Microsoft Sentinel Describe threat protection with Microsoft Defender XDR This domain tests mapping a described attack surface to the right named product across a long Defender and Sentinel lineup. Candidates who can't match which Defender product covers a surface lose the most marks in the whole exam. Build a one-line table of every Defender and Sentinel product before starting practice questions here. Describe the capabilities of Microsoft compliance solutions Published weight 20–25% 84 exam-scoped practice questions in the app Explore Compliance topics Describe Microsoft Service Trust Portal and privacy principles Describe compliance management capabilities of Microsoft Purview Describe information protection, data lifecycle management, and data governance capabilities of Microsoft Purview Describe insider risk, eDiscovery, and audit capabilities in Microsoft Purview This domain is almost entirely Microsoft Purview: compliance management, information protection, data lifecycle, insider risk, and eDiscovery. Compliance score often gets treated as a separate tool rather than the numeric output Compliance Manager actually produces. Learn compliance score as Compliance Manager's output, not a standalone product, before the exam tests that pairing. Common traps Where SC-900 candidates slip Five recurring misconceptions that trip up otherwise well-prepared SC-900 candidates, grounded in the current skills outline. Authentication and authorization answer two different questions Candidates use the two terms almost interchangeably in conversation, then mix them up the moment the exam tests them. MFA and passwordless methods authenticate identity; RBAC authorises actions. Conditional Access is the policy engine that evaluates signals and can require stronger authentication or block access. Ask whether the scenario is proving identity, assigning permissions, or evaluating access conditions before choosing a feature. Defender is a family of products, not one product SC-900 expects you to match a described surface to the specific Defender product that covers it, and the brand name alone will not get you there. Email, devices, SaaS apps, and on-premises AD signals each map to a different named Defender product. Name the exact surface in the scenario, such as email or endpoint, before choosing which Defender product answers it. Microsoft Sentinel and Defender XDR cover different scopes Both correlate security signal, so candidates treat Sentinel as just another Defender product rather than a separate platform. Sentinel is a broad SIEM and automation platform for Microsoft and non-Microsoft data. Defender XDR correlates incidents across Defender products and integrates with Sentinel. Pick Sentinel when the scenario centres on cross-environment log ingestion, analytics rules, or playbooks; pick Defender XDR for unified investigation across Defender workloads. Sensitivity labels and retention labels solve different problems in Purview Both live inside Microsoft Purview, so candidates assume one label type covers both classification and retention. Sensitivity labels protect content based on what it is; retention labels govern how long that content is kept. Pick retention over sensitivity whenever the scenario is about a legally required keep-or-delete period. Compliance score is an output, not a separate tool Candidates describe compliance score as its own product rather than a number that Compliance Manager calculates. Compliance score is the weighted output Compliance Manager produces from whichever assessments you've chosen to run. Remember compliance score reports on Compliance Manager's controls; it isn't a tool you configure on its own. 2-week revision plan Suggested SC-900 study plan Build a map of security, identity and compliance services in the first week. Use the second week for focused revision and timed practice. Security concepts Review Zero Trust. Explore defence in depth. Understand identity as a security perimeter. Microsoft Entra Review Entra ID, MFA and Conditional Access. Compare RBAC and Identity Protection. Explore Privileged Identity Management. Microsoft security services Distinguish Defender for Cloud and Defender for Endpoint. Compare Defender for Office 365 and Defender for Identity. Review how Defender XDR connects investigation signals. Compliance services Explore Purview Compliance Manager. Review labels, DLP and retention. Compare Insider Risk and Priva scenarios. Target weaker topics Run Focus Weak Spots sessions. Review explanations for missed questions. Revisit topics you have not practised recently. Timed rehearsal Complete two 45-minute Exam Simulator sessions. Review each run carefully. Record topics that need more attention. Check your progress Complete another simulator session. Look for recurring mistakes. Use the results to plan any further study. Light review Revisit your key notes. Allow time to rest. Decide whether you are ready to move ahead.
