entries.text: Guide How to pass AZ-900 Azure Fundamentals A focused two-week route through cloud concepts, core Azure services, governance, and exam-day tactics. Updated 4 September 2026 · ~8 min read Your study loop The exam What is AZ-900, and who is it for? AZ-900 earns the Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals credential, the entry point to every Azure certification path. Unlike the exams above it, it doesn't expect you to have touched the Azure portal, let alone written a line of CLI or PowerShell. It's unusual among IT certifications: account managers, sales engineers, project managers, and finance partners sit it too, to speak the same language as the engineers around them. It's also the standard first step for anyone genuinely new to cloud computing who wants proof of the basics before committing to a harder, hands-on exam such as AZ-104 . It tests whether you can describe things, not configure them — the shared responsibility model, the right Azure service for a scenario, cost, governance, and security at a conceptual level. Microsoft updated the skills outline on 14 January 2026 , so anchor your study to the current version rather than an older syllabus you find online. Before you start Do you actually need AZ-900? AZ-900 is not a formal prerequisite for any other Microsoft certification, including AZ-104, so the real question is not "can I skip it" but "will it help me." It helps if cloud computing is genuinely new to you and you want a low-stakes way to confirm this is the right direction before an Associate-level exam. It helps if you work in a non-technical role where the certification itself is the point, or a job advert or Microsoft Partner Network requirement specifically lists it. In either case, it's a worthwhile week or two of study that never expires. It's safe to skip if you already administer Azure hands-on and can already explain a resource group, a region pair, and the difference between a virtual network and a virtual machine without looking anything up — go straight to AZ-104 . Not sure which describes you? The which Microsoft certification first guide walks through the decision. Format & domains Exam format and skills domains AZ-900 is entirely multiple choice — no drag-and-drop ordering, no hotspot clicks, no case studies. That alone makes it more approachable than the exams above it. The trade-off is that questions can still be worded precisely, so read each one carefully rather than pattern-matching on keywords. Questions Typically 35–50; varies Duration 45 minutes (65-minute seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 (scaled) Delivery Online or a test centre Validity Never expires (Fundamentals) Fee Varies by country The exam fee changes from country to country and Microsoft occasionally runs free-voucher promotions around events such as Microsoft Build, so check Microsoft's certification page for the current price where you live. The three skills domains and their weights, from the official January 2026 outline, are below. AZ-900 skills measured (January 2026 outline) Domain Weight Describe cloud concepts 25–30% Describe Azure architecture and services 35–40% Describe Azure management and governance 30–35% There is no dedicated networking or compute domain the way there is on AZ-104 — those topics sit inside "Azure architecture and services" alongside identity and storage, which is why that domain carries the heaviest weight. Cloud concepts is smallest, but it underpins the vocabulary the other two rely on, so do not skim it. Three-week study plan A realistic three-week study plan Most candidates with some general IT background pass after one to two weeks of focused study. If cloud computing is genuinely new to you, three to four weeks is more realistic. The plan below spreads three weeks across the three domains in order of weight, with the final days set aside for simulation. Cloud concepts Small in weight, but it's the vocabulary the other two domains are written in terms of, so don't rush it. Shared responsibility model; public, private, and hybrid cloud. Consumption-based pricing and serverless computing. The three service models — IaaS, PaaS, SaaS — with a real example of each. Azure architecture and services The largest domain, so it gets a full week: almost every later question assumes you already know this hierarchy. Regions, region pairs, availability zones, resource groups, subscriptions, management groups. Compute and networking: VMs, scale sets, containers, Functions, virtual networks, public versus private endpoints. Storage tiers, then identity and security: Entra ID, MFA, Conditional Access, RBAC, Zero Trust, defence-in-depth. Management, governance, and exam simulation Cover the last domain, then spend the closing days proving you're ready. Cost management, the pricing calculator, Azure Policy, resource locks. Portal versus Cloud Shell versus CLI; Azure Advisor, Service Health, Azure Monitor. Run Focus Weak Spots daily, then sit two full-length timed practice exams. Where people lose marks The hardest AZ-900 topics AZ-900 is conceptual, so nothing on it is unfair, but a handful of areas trip up beginners in particular because the wording is subtle rather than the underlying idea being difficult. Give these extra attention. Service model boundaries (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) Beginners can name the three models but stumble on who is responsible for what inside each one — the OS, the hardware, the data. Practise classifying a workload as IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS, then say out loud who patches, who manages, and who protects it. Regions, availability zones, and region pairs These three terms sound alike, and confusing them is the single most common beginner mistake on this exam. Fix the distinction: a region is a geographic area, an availability zone protects against local failure inside one, a region pair is two regions used together for disaster recovery. Identity and access terms Entra ID, MFA, Conditional Access, and RBAC live in the same domain and blur together in memory. Separate what each controls: Entra ID is the identity store, MFA proves who you are, Conditional Access decides when extra proof is needed, RBAC decides what a verified identity can do. Governance tools: Policy, locks, and Purview Questions describe a requirement and expect the one tool built for that job, not a plausible-sounding alternative. Know that Azure Policy enforces configuration rules, a resource lock blocks deletion or change, and Microsoft Purview catalogues data across the organisation. Pricing and cost management factors Two cost tools get swapped for each other, and that mix-up costs a mark that should be free. Remember the pricing calculator estimates cost before you deploy, while Azure Cost Management analyses and controls spend on what you already have. How to practise Practise the way the exam works A course video leaves you able to recognise the right answer without being able to produce it, and AZ-900 asks you to produce it against the clock. Retrieval practice : commit to an answer from memory before the explanation appears — pulling the fact back is what makes it stick. Spaced repetition : return to each topic a few days after first studying it, so details such as region pairs stay familiar as exam day approaches. Full-length, timed simulation : 45 minutes for 40 to 60 questions is roughly a minute each, comfortable if you keep moving — but the only way to know you can sustain that pace is to try it under the clock. Sit at least one full run before you book the real exam. Retrieval practice, built in Azure Mastery is the retrieval-practice habit above, packaged: original AZ-900 questions across all three domains, an adaptive plan circling back to your weak spots, and knowledge-decay alerts before a term like "region pair" fades. Exam IQ adds an on-device readiness score with a confidence range. Free to start, no account needed. Download Azure Mastery — free After you pass What's next after AZ-900? AZ-900 does not lead anywhere by itself in career terms, and that is fine — its job is to confirm the conceptual map is in place. For most people who work with technology, the natural next step is AZ-104 (Microsoft Azure Administrator) , the hands-on Associate exam most "Azure Administrator" adverts actually ask for. It's a genuine step up: where AZ-900 asks you to describe a virtual network, AZ-104 asks you to configure one, read a Bicep template, and predict what an Azure CLI command does. Give yourself a real gap between the two — most people spend four to eight weeks on AZ-104 after passing AZ-900, not a weekend. The how to pass AZ-104 guide has its own domains and a six-week plan. Interested in security or data instead? AZ-900 feeds the Security Engineer Associate path (via AZ-104 then AZ-500) as readily as it feeds AZ-104 alone — the which Microsoft certification first guide compares the starting points.

entries.text: Guide How to pass DP-900 Data Fundamentals A four-week route from core data concepts to relational, NoSQL, analytics workloads, and exam-day tactics. Updated 4 September 2026 · ~8 min read Your study loop The exam What is DP-900, and is it for you? DP-900 earns the Microsoft Certified: Azure Data Fundamentals credential — the entry-level exam for anyone working near data in Azure. Aimed at candidates with basic familiarity with relational versus non-relational data and transactional versus analytical workloads; it doesn't assume database-administration experience. Common candidates: data analysts moving into Power BI work, software engineers crossing into a data role, and product or operations partners who need to discuss data architecture credibly. It expects you to recognise scenarios , not write SQL: structured versus semi-structured versus unstructured data, OLTP versus OLAP workloads, when a lift-and-shift SQL Server beats Azure SQL Database, when to reach for Cosmos DB instead of Blob Storage. It also covers how Microsoft Fabric's analytics surface relates to Azure Synapse Analytics. Microsoft last updated the skills outline on 1 November 2024 ; DP-900 is the recommended, though optional, on-ramp to the Data and BI role-based tracks. See the full breakdown on the DP-900 study app page , or read the official outline at learn.microsoft.com . Questions Roughly 40–60, multiple choice Duration 45 minutes (65-minute seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 (scaled) Delivery Online or a test centre Validity Never expires (Fundamentals) Fee Varies by country The exam fee changes from country to country, so check Microsoft's certification page for the price where you live. Format & domains Skills domains and weights Four domains, weighted from Microsoft's November 2024 outline. Two of them — core concepts and analytics — are tied for the largest share, so plan your time accordingly rather than splitting study evenly across all four. DP-900 skills measured (November 2024 outline) Domain Weight Describe core data concepts 25–30% Identify considerations for relational data on Azure 20–25% Describe considerations for non-relational data on Azure 15–20% Describe an analytics workload on Azure 25–30% Core data concepts is the conceptual base: structured versus semi-structured versus unstructured data, common file formats such as CSV, JSON, Parquet, and Avro, database types from relational to graph, and OLTP versus OLAP. Analytics workloads is the applied end: Microsoft Fabric and Azure Synapse Analytics, ingestion with Azure Data Factory, streaming with Azure Stream Analytics, and Power BI. Together they're over half the exam, so treat the two smaller domains — relational and non-relational data — as focused sprints rather than the main event. Four-week study plan A realistic four-week study plan Most candidates with some IT background pass DP-900 after one to two weeks of focused study. If data and cloud concepts are genuinely new to you, stretch that to three or four weeks — the plan below assumes the longer end and maps one week onto each domain, finishing with simulation. Core data concepts The largest domain, and the conceptual base everything else assumes. Structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data; file formats including CSV, JSON, Parquet, Avro. Database types from relational and key-value to document, graph, and columnar. OLTP versus OLAP; the four classic data roles — administrator, engineer, analyst, scientist. Relational data on Azure Drill scenario questions like "single-tenant lift-and-shift" against "cloud-native serverless app" until the right service is automatic. Relational concepts: tables, indexes, views, normalisation. The SQL Server family: Azure SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, SQL Server on Azure VMs. Open-source options: PostgreSQL and MySQL on Azure. Non-relational data on Azure The smallest domain, so it should take the least time. Azure Cosmos DB and its API options: NoSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table. Azure Storage for non-relational data: Blob containers, file shares, Data Lake Storage Gen2, table storage. Practise matching an access pattern to the right storage tier. Analytics workloads and simulation Tied for the largest domain, then the week you prove you're ready. Modern data warehousing; Microsoft Fabric and Azure Synapse Analytics. Ingestion with Azure Data Factory and Synapse pipelines; streaming with Azure Stream Analytics. Power BI Desktop versus Service; two full-length timed simulator runs before you book. Where people lose marks The hardest DP-900 topics In DP-900, similar service names can hide different purposes. Practise choosing a service for the scenario, especially in the areas below. Relational versus non-relational trade-offs Both a relational and a non-relational store can technically hold the same data, and the question tests whether you know why one still fits better. Judge schema rigidity, query patterns, and scale needs, not just whether the data could squeeze in either way. The Azure SQL service triangle Azure SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, and SQL Server on Azure VMs solve overlapping problems at different levels of control. Match the deciding factor: cloud-native app to Azure SQL Database, near-verbatim lift-and-shift to Managed Instance, OS-level access needs to the VM option. Cosmos DB's API options Cosmos DB is one service with five API surfaces, and DP-900 describes a workload shape and asks which API fits it. Memorise the pairing: document storage to NoSQL or MongoDB, wide-column to Cassandra, graph traversal to Gremlin, key-value to Table. Batch versus streaming ingestion "Near real-time dashboards" and "nightly reporting" are testing whether you reach for the right ingestion pattern, not just whether you can name both services. Azure Data Factory and Synapse pipelines move data on a schedule (batch); Azure Stream Analytics processes it continuously as it arrives (streaming). Choosing an analytics service Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse Analytics, and Power BI overlap in places, and the naming does candidates no favours. Fabric is the unified platform built around OneLake, Synapse Analytics is the underlying data-warehousing engine, and Power BI Desktop authors reports that Power BI Service publishes. How to practise Practise the way the exam works Courses and videos leave you able to spot a correct answer, not summon one, yet DP-900's scenario questions want the summoning done under mild time pressure. Retrieval practice : give your answer from memory before checking the explanation — quick recognition is half the battle on a vocabulary-heavy paper like this. Spaced repetition : return to each domain just as it begins to fade rather than covering it once and moving on; four domains is easy to hold for a day and harder across four weeks. Full-length simulation : a timed, mixed-domain run at DP-900's actual 45-minute length is the only way to find out whether you can keep pace across 40 to 60 questions. Do at least two runs before you book, and review every wrong answer properly rather than just noting the score. Case-study-style linked questions do appear, mostly around storage and identity, so make sure one simulator run includes them. Azure Mastery rebuilds its study plan from your answer history, surfacing the weakest domains first. Tell the service names apart for good Azure Mastery writes a rationale for every option on every DP-900 question, so a wrong guess between Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance teaches you the distinction. Exam IQ predicts your score on-device, the study plan re-targets your weak domain, and the simulator runs at the real 45-minute length. Free to start, works offline. Download Azure Mastery — free After DP-900 What's next after DP-900 DP-900 does not expire and is not a formal prerequisite for anything — treat it as the on-ramp that confirms data is the right direction before two or three months on a role-based exam. To run and secure Azure SQL workloads in production — high availability, disaster recovery, performance, security — the next stop is DP-300 (Azure Database Administrator Associate) , which builds on the relational-data domain here but expects hands-on T-SQL and configuration. To build the pipelines that load and shape data , pick a platform: DP-700 (Fabric Data Engineer Associate) goes deep on Microsoft Fabric — Dataflows Gen2, notebooks and PySpark, Eventstream, Lakehouse and Warehouse optimisation. DP-750 (Azure Databricks Data Engineer Associate) covers the same ground on Databricks instead — Lakeflow Connect, Unity Catalog governance, Spark job tuning. Most engineers pick one platform to match their employer's stack; some eventually sit both. Not sure administration or engineering fits, or whether Azure's general infrastructure track suits you better first? The Which Microsoft certification first? guide compares the Azure, security, and data tracks.

entries.text: Guide How to pass SC-500 : Cloud and AI Security Engineer A practical six-week route through identity, storage, network, compute, and AI security — plus posture management — for Microsoft's newest security engineering exam, the exam that replaced AZ-500. Updated 4 September 2026 · ~10 min read Your study loop The exam What is SC-500, and is it for you? SC-500 earns the Microsoft Certified: Cloud and AI Security Engineer Associate credential, spanning identity, network, application, data, and compute security across cloud and hybrid environments. Targets security engineers who now also help secure the platforms, data, and infrastructure behind AI workloads, not just traditional infrastructure. It's the direct successor to AZ-500 (Microsoft Azure Security Engineer), which retired on 31 August 2026 — most of its identity, storage, database, network, and compute security content carries over largely unchanged. What's genuinely new is a dedicated Secure compute for AI skill group: Purview Data Security Posture Management for Copilot, Microsoft Entra Agent ID, AI Gateway in API Management, Defender for AI Services, and Foundry guardrails. Became generally available on 1 July 2026 , so it's still a young credential and the AI-security content especially has little third-party prep material. Expect scenario-driven questions built around GA features, with occasional coverage of commonly used preview capabilities. Skills measured were last confirmed on 13 May 2026 — anchor your study there, not to older AZ-500 material, which covers a different, retired exam. Format & domains Exam format and skills domains SC-500 mixes question styles: single-answer and multi-select items, ordering tasks around a configuration or investigation workflow, and case studies that group several questions around one security-engineering scenario. Questions Roughly 40–60 Duration 100 minutes (120-minute seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 (scaled) Delivery Online or a test centre Validity Renew free every year Fee Varies by country The exam fee changes from country to country, so check Microsoft's certification page for the price where you live. The four skills domains and their weights, from the official May 2026 outline, are below. SC-500 skills measured (May 2026 outline) Domain Weight Manage identity, access, and governance 20–25% Secure storage, databases, and networking 25–30% Secure compute 20–25% Manage and monitor security posture 20–25% Secure storage, databases, and networking is the largest single domain, covering Defender for Storage and Databases, Azure SQL auditing, private endpoints and Private Link, network security groups, and Azure Firewall. Secure compute is where the AI-security content lives — the clearest differentiator from AZ-500 — and deserves focused attention even though its weight matches the other two remaining domains. Six-week study plan A realistic six-week study plan Use the six-week plan below as a starting point if you already administer Azure security day to day; extend it when Microsoft Sentinel, Entra Agent ID, or the AI-security controls are unfamiliar. It gives the largest domain — storage, databases, and networking — two full weeks, with the remaining three domains taking one week each. Manage identity, access, and governance The smallest domain, covered in full this week. Entra ID: PIM, Conditional Access, MFA and passwordless, application identities, OAuth consent, managed identities. Key Vault: deployment, access policies, firewall rules, Defender for Key Vault. Governance: Azure Policy, Defender for Cloud compliance standards, resource locks, RBAC, IaC controls. Secure storage and databases The largest domain starts here. Storage: firewall rules, Defender for Storage, access policies. Databases: Azure SQL platform-level security, database auditing, Defender for Databases. Secure Azure network services Networking closes out the largest domain. NSGs and ASGs; Virtual Network Manager access policies; Virtual WAN security; VPN connections. Entra Private Access; private endpoints and Private Link for PaaS; Azure Firewall; effective rules via Network Watcher. Secure compute: AI, servers, and the application platform Give the headline addition over AZ-500 a deliberate deep dive before the more familiar compute topics. AI security: Purview DSPM for Copilot and AI apps, real-time protection for Copilot Studio agents, Conditional Access and blast-radius analysis for Entra Agent ID, AI Gateway, Defender for AI Services, Foundry guardrails. Servers and VMs: disk encryption, Azure Bastion, just-in-time access, Azure Arc, Defender for Servers, secure boot and vTPM. Application platform: Defender for Containers, AKS, Container Apps, Functions, Logic Apps, App Service, WAF. Manage and monitor security posture Three tools, one domain. Defender for Cloud CSPM, compliance frameworks, workload protection plans, multicloud AWS/GCP connectors. Sentinel ingestion: workspaces, data connectors, syslog/CEF, Windows event collection, automation rules and playbooks. Microsoft Security Copilot: workspaces, permissions, plugins, agents. Review and exam simulation Revisit the control-layering distinctions the exam leans on hardest, then prove you're ready. Which Defender for Cloud plan covers which resource, and which network-access control fits which pattern. Drill your weakest domain daily, then sit two full-length timed practice runs before you book. Focus areas The hardest SC-500 topics SC-500 covers many security controls with similar names. Focus on these five areas and practise choosing the control that fits each threat. The AI-security control set Purview DSPM, Entra Agent ID Conditional Access, AI Gateway, Defender for AI Services, and Foundry guardrails all touch AI workloads but stop different threats. Match the named risk to the one control that addresses it: data overexposure, agent identity misuse, model-endpoint abuse, or runtime prompt attacks. Private network access patterns Private endpoints, Private Link, Entra Private Access, and Virtual Network Manager all restrict access differently. Pick the one that fits the pattern — a PaaS resource, a user outside Azure, or centralised policy across many networks — not the one you know best. Which Defender for Cloud plan covers what CSPM and the individual plans for Storage, Databases, Servers, Containers, and Key Vault overlap in the dashboard but protect different resource types. Questions naming a specific resource and threat expect the specific plan, not a generic "enable Defender for Cloud" answer. Governance layering: policy, RBAC, and locks Azure Policy, RBAC, resource locks, and Key Vault access policies each stop a different kind of misconfiguration. SC-500 tests which layer actually prevents the scenario: an accidental deletion, an overprivileged assignment, or a non-compliant resource being created. Matching a Sentinel ingestion method to the source Built-in connectors, syslog/CEF forwarding, data-collection-rule Windows Event collection, and custom log tables all get data in, but each suits a different source and licensing model. Read a source description and name the correct ingestion path rather than defaulting to whichever is most familiar. How to practise Practise the way the exam works SC-500 rewards matching a control or plan to a scenario, a skill built through practice more than reading. After reading Defender for Cloud documentation, practise matching a control or plan to a scenario, choosing your answer before reading the explanation. Give the AI-security topics extra time, especially if most of your experience comes from AZ-500. Revisit all four domains with spaced repetition: identity, storage and networking, compute, and posture management. Complete at least two full-length timed practice tests before booking, and check whether your accuracy holds up in the later questions. Review each wrong answer afterwards to decide what needs more practice. Azure Mastery rebuilds its study plan from your answer history, surfacing the weakest domains first. New AI-security content, the same rigour Azure Mastery writes a rationale for every option on every SC-500 question, so a wrong call on Purview DSPM versus Defender for AI Services teaches you the distinction, not just the score. Exam IQ gives you an on-device readiness score with a confidence range, and the study plan keeps circling back to your weak domain. Free to start, works offline. Download Azure Mastery — free Exam day Tactics for exam day A few habits protect the marks you've already earned. Sitting online? Run the system check the day before and clear your desk — proctors ask you to show the room first. Arrive early either way; a rushed start eats into your focus during the dense scenario questions. Budget roughly ninety seconds to two minutes per question, and flag anything you pause on with mark-for-review . Read every network or Defender-for-Cloud question twice — the trap is usually one scope, resource type, or plan name. Answer everything inside a case study before you advance; you generally cannot return to one once you leave it. Remember the pass mark is 700 out of 1000, scaled. An unfamiliar configuration isn't a disaster: make your call and keep moving.

entries.text: Guide How to pass SC-900 Security Fundamentals A four-week route through security, Entra, Microsoft security and compliance solutions, plus exam-day tactics. Updated 4 September 2026 · ~9 min read Your study loop The exam What is SC-900, and is it for you? SC-900 earns the Microsoft Certified: Security, Compliance, and Identity Fundamentals credential, the entry-level exam for Microsoft's whole security stack across Azure and Microsoft 365. Deliberately written for a wide audience: business stakeholders evaluating security procurement, IT generalists moving toward a security role, and students building a foundation before a specialism. No technical background needed — it doesn't ask you to configure a Conditional Access policy or write a Sentinel query. It asks you to recognise the right concept or product for a scenario: which control enforces Zero Trust, which Defender product covers this surface, which Purview tool meets this requirement. That makes it a genuine Fundamentals exam rather than a scaled-down Associate one. Microsoft updated the skills outline on 7 November 2025 and refreshes it periodically as its security products evolve, so anchor your study to the live objectives. Sits alongside AZ-900 and AI-901 as one of the three main Fundamentals exams, and is the recommended, though not required, on-ramp to the Security Operations, Identity, and Cybersecurity Architect tracks. Format & domains Exam format and skills domains SC-900 is entirely multiple choice — no drag-and-drop ordering, no hotspot screenshots, no case studies. What it lacks in question variety it makes up for in breadth: four domains cover everything from abstract security concepts to five distinct Microsoft Defender products. Questions Typically 35–50; varies Duration 45 minutes (65-minute seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 (scaled) Delivery Online or a test centre Validity Never expires (Fundamentals) Fee Varies by country The exam fee changes from country to country, so check Microsoft's certification page for the price where you live. The four skills domains and their weights, from the official November 2025 outline, are below. SC-900 skills measured (November 2025 outline) Domain Weight Describe the concepts of security, compliance, and identity 10–15% Describe the capabilities of Microsoft Entra 25–30% Describe the capabilities of Microsoft security solutions 35–40% Describe the capabilities of Microsoft compliance solutions 20–25% Microsoft security solutions and Microsoft Entra together account for roughly two-thirds of the exam, so give them the largest share of your revision time. The concepts domain is smallest, but skipping it is a mistake — Zero Trust and shared responsibility are the vocabulary the other three domains assume you already have. Four-week study plan A realistic four-week study plan If you already work in IT, one to two weeks of focused revision is enough. If security and cloud concepts are new, four weeks gives each domain proper room. Compress it if Conditional Access and Zero Trust feel familiar; stretch it if this is your first Microsoft exam. Each week below maps onto the domains by weight. Security, compliance, and identity concepts The smallest domain, but it underpins everything that follows. Shared responsibility model, defence-in-depth, Zero Trust, encryption versus hashing. Identity as the security perimeter; authentication versus authorisation. Identity providers, directory services and Active Directory, federation. Microsoft Entra The biggest domain, and the most scenario-heavy. Entra ID identity types: member, guest, hybrid. Authentication: MFA, passwordless sign-in, password protection. Access management with Conditional Access and Entra RBAC; governance through Identity Protection, PIM, and entitlement management. Microsoft security solutions The largest domain by weight, and where the product names pile up. Core Azure security: NSGs, Azure Firewall, DDoS Protection, Web Application Firewall. The Defender family: Cloud, Endpoint, Office 365, Identity, and XDR. Microsoft Sentinel for SIEM and SOAR, plus Defender Threat Intelligence. Microsoft compliance solutions and simulation Cover the last domain, then spend the closing days under exam conditions. Purview's compliance portal, Compliance Manager, compliance score. Sensitivity labels, retention policies, records management, data loss prevention; insider risk; Microsoft Priva. Drill your weakest domain daily, then sit two full-length timed simulations before you book. Where people lose marks The hardest SC-900 topics SC-900 tests concepts and precise definitions. Give the areas below extra attention, especially when similar terms are easy to confuse. Authentication versus authorisation These two terms are used almost interchangeably in everyday speech, and the exam relies on you keeping them apart. Authentication proves who you are; authorisation decides what you're allowed to do once proven — label every scenario as one or the other before you check the answer. Zero Trust Candidates memorise the phrase "Zero Trust" but not the three principles behind it, and stall when a question asks which principle a control demonstrates. Learn verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, and assume breach by name, then practise matching real controls like Conditional Access to the one each supports. The shared responsibility model Responsibility shifts with the service model, and questions describe one control and ask whose job it is under a given model. On-premises: you own everything. IaaS: Microsoft takes the physical layers. SaaS: Microsoft owns almost everything except your data and identities. Telling the Defender products apart Microsoft security solutions is the largest domain, and the five-strong Defender family is where most marks are lost. Write a one-line description of each in your own words: Cloud protects workloads, Endpoint protects devices, Office 365 protects email, Identity protects on-premises AD signals, XDR ties detections together. How to practise Practise the way the exam works SC-900 tests recall of specific product names under time pressure, a skill videos alone don't build. Use questions alongside videos and Microsoft Learn modules; answer from memory before reading the explanation, then return to the topic a few days later. That spacing helps you retain what you studied earlier in the plan rather than losing it to the domains that follow. Complete at least two full-length timed practice tests before booking, recalling vocabulary from all four domains across 40 to 60 questions in 45 minutes. Review every wrong answer as well as your overall score. Keep the Defender family straight Azure Mastery drills every SC-900 domain with a rationale on every option, so mixing up Defender for Cloud and Defender for Identity teaches you the distinction, not just costs a mark. Exam IQ adds an on-device readiness score, the plan re-targets your weak domain, and the simulator runs at blueprint weight. Free to start, works offline. Download Azure Mastery — free Exam day Tactics for exam day A few habits keep 45 minutes from feeling rushed. Sitting online? Run the system check the day before and clear your desk — the proctor sweeps the webcam across the room before you start. Arrive early either way, whether that's logging in ahead of time or reaching the test centre with room to settle. Budget 45 to 65 seconds per question, and flag anything you hesitate on with mark-for-review instead of losing a minute on it early. Read scenario questions twice. SC-900 hides the answer in a subtle word choice — "hybrid" versus "guest" identity, "detect" versus "prevent". Remember the pass mark is 700 out of 1000, scaled. An unfamiliar term isn't a disaster: make your call and move on. After SC-900 What's next after SC-900 SC-900 does not lock you into one path. It is the shared on-ramp for two different Associate-level directions, and which one fits depends on whether you want to defend against attacks or build and secure the platform itself. For day-to-day security operations — investigating alerts, hunting threats in Microsoft Sentinel, working inside Defender XDR — SC-200 (Security Operations Analyst Associate) is the natural next step. For engineering and securing cloud and AI workloads rather than monitoring them, look at SC-500 , Microsoft's credential that replaced AZ-500 when it retired on 31 August 2026. Both expect hands-on configuration in a way SC-900 deliberately does not. Not sure which track to commit to, or whether to pair SC-900 with a cloud-fundamentals exam first? The guides below walk through the decision. Every other exam's guide lives at Azure certification guides .

See exactly what SC-500 kept, what it added, and what happens to an AZ-500 credential you already hold. Updated 4 September 2026 · ~9 min read One path is still open Quick answer SC-500 or AZ-500: the short version This isn't really a choice any more. AZ-500 retired on 31 August 2026, so SC-500 is the only cloud-security Associate exam you can currently book. What's worth understanding is what changed, and what an existing AZ-500 credential is still worth. New to cloud security? Sit SC-500 SC-500 (Microsoft Certified: Cloud and AI Security Engineer Associate) is the current, bookable exam for anyone starting a cloud security career today. It keeps the core Azure security-engineering content AZ-500 tested and adds a full domain of AI-workload security that AZ-500 never covered. Already hold AZ-500? It stays on your transcript Passing AZ-500 before its retirement date remains valid — Microsoft does not revoke certifications when the underlying exam retires. What it does mean is that AZ-500 itself can no longer be renewed. See "If you hold AZ-500" below for what that means in practice and how much of your existing knowledge carries straight over. Both exams lead to a "Microsoft Certified" Associate credential in cloud security; the difference below is entirely about scope and timing, not prestige. Side by side SC-500 vs AZ-500 at a glance AZ-500's figures below describe the exam as it stood before it retired; they're kept here for comparison, not as a live booking option. SC-500 and AZ-500 compared Category SC-500 AZ-500 (retired) Credential Microsoft Certified: Cloud and AI Security Engineer Associate Microsoft Certified: Azure Security Engineer Associate Best for Anyone starting a cloud-and-AI security career today — the only current bookable option Historical reference only — credential holders keep it, but it can no longer be booked or renewed Domains 4: identity, access & governance; storage, databases & networking; compute (incl. AI security); posture management 4: identity & access; networking; compute, storage & databases; Defender for Cloud & Sentinel Format 40–60 questions, 100 minutes (120-minute seat) 40–60 questions, 100 minutes (120-minute seat) Question style Multiple choice and multi-select scenario questions, often a config snippet or an attack signal to interpret Multiple choice and multi-select scenario questions, the same config-and-signal format SC-500 inherited Pass score 700 / 1000 700 / 1000 Typical prep time Four to six weeks with AZ-104-level Azure experience; add time for the AI-security skill group if that's new to you Four to six weeks with hands-on Azure security experience, while the exam was still active Renewal Renew annually, free online assessment Was annual while active — no longer renewable now the exam has retired Skills outline Outline effective 13 May 2026 Outline effective 22 January 2026 (final version before retirement) Exam fees vary by country. Read the official Microsoft outlines: the SC-500 study guide covers current registration and pricing, and the AZ-500 study guide is kept online as a reference even though the exam itself has retired. What SC-500 actually tests What SC-500 actually tests SC-500 covers the same operational ground AZ-500 did — identity, networking, compute, storage, and Defender for Cloud — and folds AI-workload security into the compute domain rather than treating it as an afterthought. SC-500 skills measured (outline effective 13 May 2026) Domain Weight Manage identity, access & governance 20–25% Secure storage, databases & networking 25–30% Secure compute 20–25% Manage & monitor security posture 20–25% Identity and governance covers Privileged Identity Management, Conditional Access, and Key Vault, alongside Azure Policy and RBAC remediation. Storage/databases/networking, the largest domain, is largely continuous with AZ-500's networking and storage material: NSGs, Private Link, Azure Firewall, Defender for Storage and Databases. Secure compute diverges hardest from AZ-500: alongside disk encryption, Bastion, and Defender for Servers and Containers, it adds a dedicated AI-security skill group — Entra Agent ID, Defender for AI Services, Foundry guardrails, AI Gateway in API Management, Purview DSPM for Copilot. Posture management rolls up Defender CSPM, multicloud connectors, Microsoft Sentinel ingestion, and Microsoft Security Copilot into one domain rather than one oversized 30–35% block. What AZ-500 tested What AZ-500 tested (retired 31 August 2026) Kept here as a reference for anyone comparing what they already studied against SC-500's current outline, not as an active exam guide. AZ-500 skills measured (final outline, effective 22 January 2026) Domain Weight Secure identity & access 15–20% Secure networking 20–25% Secure compute, storage & databases 20–25% Secure Azure using Defender for Cloud & Sentinel 30–35% Identity and access covered role assignments, PIM, Conditional Access, and Microsoft Entra app registrations and managed identities. Networking covered NSGs, Virtual Network Manager, Virtual WAN, private access patterns, and Azure Firewall. Compute, storage, and databases covered VM and AKS security, storage access control, and Azure SQL protections including Transparent Data Encryption. Defender for Cloud and Sentinel, the largest domain by far, covered governance policy, Secure Score remediation, threat protection plans, and hands-on Sentinel configuration including data connectors and analytics rules. Three of these four domains map closely onto SC-500's current outline; the fourth is where SC-500 now spends part of its weight on AI security instead. Prerequisite question Is there a prerequisite for SC-500? No formal one. SC-500 doesn't require another certification before you can book it, in the same way AZ-500 never did. Microsoft's own guidance recommends practical experience administering Azure and hybrid environments and strong familiarity with Microsoft Entra ID before attempting it. Azure Mastery's certification pathing lists AZ-104 as a recommended, not required, lead-in — exactly as it did for AZ-500. SC-500 doesn't currently unlock anything further up the security track on its own; Microsoft's published prerequisite guidance for SC-100 (Cybersecurity Architect Expert) doesn't list SC-500 as an accepted route as of this guide's last update — check the official SC-100 requirements directly, since Microsoft updates prerequisite lists independently of exam retirements. Deciding whether SC-900 (Security, Compliance, and Identity Fundamentals) is worth sitting first? It's optional conceptual groundwork, exactly as it was for AZ-500, mainly useful if security terminology itself is new to you. Career value How SC-500 changes what the credential signals SC-500 signals everything AZ-500 did, plus a claim AZ-500 never made. AZ-500 signalled "Cloud Security Engineer" or "Azure Security Specialist" — someone who could lock down identity, networking, compute, and storage, and run day-to-day operations in Defender for Cloud and Sentinel. SC-500 signals that same operational competence, plus the ability to extend those controls to the AI systems now running inside the organisation, from Copilot agents to Foundry-hosted models. That AI-security scope is the reason SC-500 exists rather than a straight AZ-500 renewal cycle: "who governs what an AI agent can access" became a real operational question AZ-500's outline had no domain to answer. Hiring managers posting "Cloud Security Engineer" or "Cloud and AI Security" roles in 2026 increasingly ask for that AI-specific coverage explicitly. Neither guarantees a role or a pay rise; what SC-500 does is keep the credential current and renewable, which AZ-500 can no longer do. If you hold AZ-500 What happens to an AZ-500 credential you already hold Your certification stays on your Microsoft transcript exactly as it is. Microsoft does not retroactively remove or downgrade a credential because the exam that produced it has since retired — the "Microsoft Certified: Azure Security Engineer Associate" line is permanent proof of what you passed and when. What changes is renewal: assessments are no longer available once a certification's exam has retired, so AZ-500 has no ongoing free annual renewal path. The entry stays on your transcript as a record, but there's no mechanism left to formally refresh it against a current skills outline. The practical route for staying current is SC-500. Three of AZ-500's four domains — identity and access, networking, and compute/storage/databases — map closely onto SC-500's identity, storage/database/networking, and compute domains, so a holder isn't starting from zero. The genuinely new material sits in two places: the AI-security skill group inside Secure Compute, and Microsoft Security Copilot inside posture management. Everything else is a change of emphasis and consolidation, not new content to learn from scratch. Bring AZ-500 knowledge into SC-500 practice Azure Mastery's SC-500 question bank is mapped to the current outline domain by domain, so you can see exactly which questions cover ground you already know from AZ-500 and which cover the new AI-security material. It has its own on-device Exam IQ readiness score and a full-length exam simulator, and works offline with no account required to start. Download Azure Mastery — free

entries.text: Guide SC-900 vs AZ-900 : security or cloud first? Compare cloud fundamentals with security fundamentals and choose the first exam that fits your role. Updated 4 September 2026 · ~8 min read Pick the right lens Quick answer Which one should you sit first? If you only have time to prepare for one Fundamentals exam right now, the short version comes down to what your next role actually needs. Pick AZ-900 if… You want the broad grounding: cloud service models, Azure's region and subscription structure, core compute and storage, cost management and governance. It's the standard on-ramp toward Azure Administrator ( AZ-104 ) and most general infrastructure roles. Pick SC-900 if… Your near-term work touches identity, compliance, or the security stack — Entra ID, Defender products, Purview, or Sentinel. It's the on-ramp toward the security-analyst and identity-administrator associate tracks. Neither is a formal prerequisite for the other, and neither certification expires once you pass, so there's no real penalty for choosing the "wrong" one first if your role changes direction later. The distinction that actually matters is what your next job needs: general cloud administration, or security, compliance, and identity. Side by side SC-900 and AZ-900 compared Strip away the domain content and the two exams are built on the same skeleton: both are online-proctorable, both run to the same length, and both use the same 700-out-of-1000 passing bar. The difference is entirely in what they ask you to know. SC-900 vs AZ-900 at a glance Category SC-900 AZ-900 Full name Microsoft Certified: Security, Compliance, and Identity Fundamentals Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals Focus Security, compliance, and identity concepts across Azure and Microsoft 365 General cloud computing concepts and core Azure services Skills domains 4 domains 3 domains Largest domain Microsoft security solutions (35–40%) Azure architecture and services (35–40%) Questions 40–60, multiple choice 40–60, multiple choice Duration 45 minutes (65-minute seat time) 45 minutes (65-minute seat time) Pass score 700 / 1000 700 / 1000 Validity Doesn't expire Doesn't expire Delivery Online or a test centre Online or a test centre Typical next step SC-200 or SC-300 (Associate) AZ-104 (Associate) Exam pricing varies by country for both, so check Microsoft's SC-900 and AZ-900 certification pages for the fee where you live rather than trusting a number you read elsewhere. Under the hood What each exam actually tests Compare the domain lists below to see which Fundamentals exam fits the work you want to do. AZ-900: cloud concepts, architecture, governance Its first domain covers why cloud computing exists at all — the shared responsibility model, public versus private versus hybrid cloud, consumption-based pricing, and the IaaS/PaaS/SaaS service models. Its largest domain covers Azure's actual architecture: regions, availability zones, subscriptions, and management groups, plus compute, networking, and storage services. Identity and security get one section inside that domain — Entra ID basics, MFA, Conditional Access, RBAC, Zero Trust, a mention of Defender for Cloud — but it stays at "what is this," not implementation detail. The final domain covers cost management, Azure Policy, resource locks, and monitoring tools such as Azure Monitor. AZ-900 skills measured Domain Weight Describe cloud concepts 25–30% Describe Azure architecture and services 35–40% Describe Azure management and governance 30–35% SC-900: security, compliance, and identity capabilities Opens with the concepts domain everything else leans on: the shared responsibility model again, paired with defence-in-depth, Zero Trust, and the difference between authentication and authorisation. From there it goes deep rather than wide: a quarter to nearly a third of the exam is Microsoft Entra alone — identity types, authentication methods, Conditional Access, Entra roles, Identity Protection, Privileged Identity Management. Microsoft security solutions, the largest domain, covers Azure network security tools (NSGs, Azure Firewall, DDoS Protection), the whole Microsoft Defender family, and Microsoft Sentinel for SIEM and SOAR. The final domain is compliance: Microsoft Purview, sensitivity labels and data lifecycle management, insider risk management, and Microsoft Priva. SC-900 skills measured Domain Weight Concepts of security, compliance, and identity 10–15% Capabilities of Microsoft Entra 25–30% Capabilities of Microsoft security solutions 35–40% Capabilities of Microsoft compliance solutions 20–25% The overlap Where SC-900 and AZ-900 actually overlap The two exams share more conceptual ground than their domain lists suggest, even though neither is a prerequisite for the other. Both introduce the shared responsibility model early: AZ-900 treats it as the baseline distinction between what Microsoft manages and what you manage, and SC-900 builds its opening domain directly on the same idea. Both introduce Zero Trust and defence-in-depth — AZ-900 mentions them briefly inside its architecture domain, SC-900 treats them as core concepts from the first domain onward. Microsoft Entra ID is the clearest shared thread: AZ-900 introduces it at a glance inside a broader "identity, access, and security" section, while SC-900 dedicates a quarter to nearly a third of the exam to it. The pattern repeats with Microsoft Defender for Cloud : AZ-900 name-checks it once, SC-900 treats it as one entry point into a much larger security solutions domain covering the whole Defender family plus Sentinel. The short version: AZ-900 gives you the vocabulary, SC-900 gives you the depth. Already passed one? Expect a handful of familiar terms in the other, not a free pass on study time. Doing both Which one first, if you want both eventually Plenty of people end up sitting both exams over time, especially in roles that straddle infrastructure and security. General Azure administration now or soon? Take AZ-900 first — it establishes the resource-hierarchy vocabulary SC-900 assumes lightly rather than teaches. Security, compliance, or identity the actual target role? SC-900 first is fine too — it's self-contained and needs only conceptual awareness of the cloud, not Azure operational knowledge. Genuinely undecided? Most people study AZ-900 first because it's the broader on-ramp — more of Microsoft's other Fundamentals and Associate certifications assume its vocabulary. Either way, avoid sitting both in the same fortnight — the two outlines only overlap on a handful of concepts, and cramming both into one short block blurs the material rather than reinforcing it. Still not sure which certification or order fits? Which Microsoft certification first? walks through the wider decision. Career paths Where each path leads next Each Fundamentals exam opens onto a different associate-level branch. After AZ-900, the associate-level credential most job postings actually mean is AZ-104 (Azure Administrator Associate) — hands-on subscription, identity, storage, compute, and networking administration, from where the expert tracks branch toward architecture or DevOps engineering. After SC-900, there are two natural branches depending on which half interested you more: SC-200 (Security Operations Analyst Associate) if the Microsoft security solutions domain — Defender, Sentinel — was the more engaging half. SC-300 (Identity and Access Administrator Associate) if the Microsoft Entra domain was more your speed; both feed into SC-100 (Cybersecurity Architect Expert) further up the security track. Security engineering specifically the goal? AZ-500 retired on 31 August 2026 and replaced by SC-500 (Cloud and AI Security Engineer Associate), which also pairs with SC-900 on the way in — so aim for SC-500, SC-200, or SC-300, not the retired AZ-500.

entries.text: Guide Which Microsoft certification should you get first? Match Azure, security, data, AI, analytics, or development to your role — then see the next credential on each path. Updated 4 September 2026 · ~8 min read Choose by destination The short answer Start with AZ-900, unless you already know your track If you want one safe recommendation, it is AZ-900 (Microsoft Azure Fundamentals) . It teaches the shared vocabulary every other Azure exam quietly assumes you already have: what a region and an availability zone are, how subscriptions and resource groups nest, and the services you'll meet again and again. It doesn't expire, and most people can prepare for it in a couple of weeks — a cheap, permanent foundation and a low-pressure way to confirm cloud work suits you before a longer study run. The one caveat: AZ-900 is a starting point, not a career goal . On its own it won't get you an Azure job; it gets you ready for the associate certification that will. Already know the field you want? Don't default to AZ-900 out of habit — each track has its own Fundamentals exam through the lens you care about: SC-900 for security, DP-900 for data, AI-901 for AI. Already administer Azure day to day? You can skip Fundamentals entirely and sit an associate exam first. The section below maps each starting point to a goal. Decide by goal Pick your first exam by where you are heading Microsoft's role-based certifications are organised into tracks. The cleanest way to choose is to name the job you want, take that track's Fundamentals exam to build the map, then move to the associate that hiring managers actually recruit for. Here is the whole ladder at a glance. Where to start, and where it leads, by goal If you want to… Start with Then aim for Run cloud infrastructure (IT ops, sysadmin) AZ-900 AZ-104 Work in security, identity, and compliance SC-900 SC-200 / SC-500 Work with data and databases DP-900 DP-300 / DP-700 Build with AI and machine learning AI-901 AI-103 Analyse business data (low-code, reporting) PL-300 PL-300 Write and ship code on Azure GH-900 AI-200 IT operations and administration The most common cloud entry path: start with AZ-900 for the concepts, then move to AZ-104 (Azure Administrator) , the associate that maps to real "Cloud Administrator" roles. AZ-104 is hands-on: managing identities and RBAC, configuring storage and virtual networks, and deploying VMs, rather than just describing them. Security, identity, and compliance Begin with SC-900 , which covers Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Defender, and Microsoft Purview at a conceptual level. From there, SC-200 (Security Operations Analyst) suits a SOC or threat-hunting role, while SC-500 (Azure Security Engineer) — the successor to the retired AZ-500 — suits engineers who secure Azure workloads directly. Data and databases Take DP-900 first for the relational, non-relational, and analytics concepts. Then choose by role: DP-300 (Database Administrator) if you run and tune managed databases, or DP-700 (Fabric Data Engineer) if you build data pipelines on Microsoft Fabric. Artificial intelligence and machine learning Start with AI-901 (Microsoft AI Fundamentals) , which now includes a dedicated generative-AI domain. Its natural next step is AI-103 (AI App and Agent Developer Associate) , which replaced the retired AI-102, for building generative AI apps and agents with Azure OpenAI and Azure AI Foundry, including retrieval-augmented generation over Azure AI Search. Business analysis and low-code If your goal is reporting and dashboards rather than infrastructure, PL-300 (Power BI Data Analyst) is a strong first certification in its own right. Associate-level but approachable, and maps directly to analyst roles, so many people take it without a Fundamentals exam first. Software development Developers new to the Microsoft ecosystem often start with GH-900 (GitHub Foundations) to cover source control and collaboration. From there, move toward AI-200 , the successor to the retired AZ-204 developer exam. Note that AZ-204 retired on 31 July 2026, so plan around AI-200 rather than starting AZ-204 now. What to expect What a Fundamentals cert does and does not get you A Fundamentals exam can give you a useful starting point. Here's what it prepares you for and where you'll need more experience. What they do get you A shared mental model and the correct names for things, which makes every later exam and real project easier to follow. A permanent credential that never expires, a cheap confidence check before a longer study run, and a genuine talking point if you're changing careers with no prior cloud experience. What they do not get you A Fundamentals certification alone doesn't demonstrate hands-on skill or guarantee a cloud job. Employers also look for practical experience and, often, an associate certification — Fundamentals exams are optional preparation, so you can book an associate exam directly if you're ready. The practical rule: if you have less than six months of hands-on experience with the platform, a Fundamentals exam is time well spent. If you already work with it daily, skip straight to the associate and save your effort for the exam that changes your CV. Side by side The four Fundamentals entry points compared AZ-900, SC-900, DP-900, and AI-901 share the same shape: multiple-choice questions, a 45-minute exam window, a 700-out-of-1000 pass mark, and no expiry. What differs is the subject matter and, because it is the broadest, how long AI-901 tends to take. The format facts below apply to all four. Questions Typically 35–50; varies Duration 45 minutes (65 min seat) Pass score 700 / 1000 (scaled) Validity Does not expire Delivery Online or a test centre Fee Varies by country What each Fundamentals exam covers, and roughly how long it takes to prepare Exam Subject flavour Typical prep AZ-900 Cloud concepts, Azure architecture and services, and Azure management and governance. The default first exam. ~2 weeks SC-900 Security, compliance, and identity concepts, and the capabilities of Microsoft Entra, Microsoft security, and Microsoft compliance solutions. ~2 weeks DP-900 Core data concepts plus relational, non-relational, and analytics workloads on Azure. ~2 weeks AI-901 AI workloads, machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and a dedicated generative-AI domain. The broadest of the four. 3–4 weeks Prep times assume a few evenings a week and some general IT familiarity; allow three to four weeks for the 900-series exams if the platform is genuinely new to you. Each exam page linked above has the full domain weights and a study plan built around them. Once you have chosen Prepare the way the exam works Build two habits alongside courses and videos. First, answer practice questions from memory before reading the explanation. Second, complete a full-length timed practice test to get used to the pace and question formats. Both help you apply what you've learned under exam conditions. You get an on-device Exam IQ score with a confidence range, an adaptive plan that targets your weak spots, and a blueprint-weighted simulator for whichever exam you choose. entries.text: Exam IQ How Exam IQ predicts your score Exam IQ estimates your certification exam score from your practice answers, on-device, with a confidence range that narrows the more it learns about you. What it is What Exam IQ is Exam IQ estimates your likely Microsoft certification exam score on your device and recommends what to study next. It updates after every question you answer. The models also estimate your ability in each exam domain, so you can see which areas need work. Knowledge-decay tracking uses the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve to flag topics you're likely to have forgotten since your last review. What it reads What the model reads The app includes a CoreML model for score prediction, with a weighted formula as a fallback if the model is unavailable. Both read the same signals from your answer history: Test scores and consistency, and your strongest and weakest domains. Question coverage and mastery across the outline. Practice-test streaks, study hours and improvement over time. Remaining weak topics and how long you've been active. Answer speed and how often you read explanations. Confidence range What the confidence range means Your predicted score comes with a confidence range: a low and a high estimate. A narrower range means the estimate is more confident, usually because you've answered more questions. A wider range means the app needs more practice data to make a more precise estimate. The app also estimates how likely you are to reach the pass mark, so you can see both your predicted score and its uncertainty. Why on-device Why it runs on-device The CoreML model and its fallback formula both run on your device. Azure Mastery does not send your answers to a server for score prediction. You can choose to sync your progress separately through your private iCloud account. Limits What it cannot do Exam IQ uses your practice in the app to estimate readiness. It cannot guarantee a pass or access Microsoft's live exam questions and scoring. Use the estimate to guide your study alongside your own judgement and hands-on experience.

entries.summary: How Azure Mastery's practice questions are written against Microsoft's published skills outlines, checked on every change, and watched weekly for drift.
entries.text: Methodology How we write and verify practice questions Every question is written against Microsoft's published exam outline, checked automatically when it changes, and watched afterwards for drift. The outline Based on the published exam outline Each question bank follows the "Skills measured" outline Microsoft publishes for that exam. We record the outline version using a hash, a digital fingerprint of the page, and keep a record of the review that checks how the questions map to its topics. Microsoft revises outlines regularly, and sometimes publishes an upcoming version ahead of its effective date. A weekly automated check compares the live outline against what shipped and flags drift. If Microsoft's new outline is not yet in effect, the check reports it as upcoming rather than treating today's content as already stale. Explain, don't trick Written to explain, not to trick Every question includes a written explanation. When a format calls for comparing options, the explanation must meet a minimum length before publication. It needs enough detail to explain why the wrong options fail as well as why the correct answer works. Multiple choice, drag-and-drop ordering, hotspot, and case studies all test skills in the published outline. The questions should test your understanding without relying on ambiguous wording. Every option Every option gets a rationale Where per-option rationales are available, each option has its own explanation. Answer Coach uses those written rationales to explain a wrong choice, so the feedback addresses the answer you selected. Before publication, automated checks scan every explanation for three defects, and all three must pass: An explanation that just labels the answer "correct" without saying why. Internal review language accidentally left in the published text. A wrong-option rationale that gives away the answer. Checked always Checked on every change Every change to a question bank runs through automated checks before it can publish: Data structure and integrity, so nothing malformed ships. The bank's mapping against the exam outline. Wording problems, such as a stem that gives away its own answer or options that just repeat the question. A failed check blocks publication outright. Several checks track a fixed maximum number of existing defects in each bank. Changes can reduce that number but cannot increase it. This prevents new edits from adding to the known problems. Watched weekly Watched weekly against Microsoft Learn Two scheduled checks run even when the content hasn't changed. Every Monday, one compares a hash of each live "Skills measured" page with the version recorded for the published bank. Differences flag an outline change for review. Once a month, the other check tests every question's "learn more" link. Microsoft Learn pages sometimes move or disappear, so this finds links that need repair. Limits What we do not claim This app is not a leaked or memorised question dump, and it contains no live exam items. Microsoft controls the real exam's content, format and scoring, none of which is available to third parties, so passing consistently here does not guarantee passing on the day. The in-app Exam IQ score is a readiness estimate built from your own practice record, not a promise — see how Exam IQ works for exactly what it measures.
